LONDON. THIJRBDIT.

_ The Whitsun recess hut betome an absolute necessity for the further existence of an unusually large section of the House. ,As }have explained in a former letter, the pressure upon members is ap-; plied over an exceptionally large area. This a neces- sary element in the application of the Closure that Ministers should have at their command a majority of 200. Thus, as the division lists show when the House has sat through the night, there have been Viler 300 present. In the last division, taken at five o'clock on Tuesday morning', no less than 338 mem- bers recorded their votes. . This is a very different state of things from the old order, when all-night sittings were kept up with an aggregate attendance of something like a hundred. The pressure upon the Speaker, the Chairman of Committees, and the officials of the House has been very serious. The bulk of members who remain to carry the Closure do not stay in the House. They come in to vote, and straightway go out to make themselves comforta- ble.. But the Speaker or the Chairman of Committees, with the officials on duty, must needs remain at their post. Mr. Courtney shows no sign of distress, ! but it is telling terribly on the Speaker: As he walked up the aisle of St. Margaret's Church on Sunday morning, his face was of a ghastly • yellow colour, startling to see. But whilst Speaker, Chairman of Committees, !officials, and the trained band of Coercionia its wel- come the holidays with unusual fervour, t must be la matter of intense relief to her Majesty's Ministers. In addition to the labour of sitting, watching. and waiting, they have labourea under the disdniraging circumstances of being personally discredited. Not I even the most uncompromising Ministerialist can ! deny that in their relations with the House Mini- sters have proved a melancholy failure. The most 'striking instance of the prevailing misfortune is 1 the First Lord of the Treasury. Mr. Smith had an exceedingly fair chance • everyone was anxious to make things pleasant for him, and to look with most favourable eye upon his efforts to fill the seat but lately occupied by Mr. Disraeli and Mr. Glad- stone. But he has blundered along in a certain placid commonplace manner that curiously aggra- vates the situation. He never by any chance stumbles on to the right course and doeswrong with a certain self-complacent air that angers the on- looker. The House has now begun to poke fun at him; a hopeless condition of affairs where tint leader of the House of Commons is concerned. On '1 Sunday, at St. Margaret's Church, when the Bishop of Ripon had viand the half-hour in the delivery of his eloquent sermon there passed along the ' crowded benches the whispered joke that Smith is going to move the Closure. All eyes were turned I towards the pew in which the good. man sat divided ' by a colleague from Mr. Gladstone. The sudden death of Mr. Blake is lamented' from all sides of the House pf Commons. He was one of the original band of Horne Rulers. He very rarely spoke though he once made a speech, which lives in the memory of everyone privileged to hear it. It happened three years ago in debate on the Irish Sunday Closing Bill. Mr. Blake supported the mea- sure, and incidenrally related a private effort of his own in the cause of temperance. He had, he in- formed the House in his gravest manner and with his delightfully unctious brogue, an uncle who I regularly took six tumblers of whisky toddy as his I day's allowance. Mr. Blake, troubled at this evil habit, resolved to write and remonstrate with hit. errant relatiVe. The following was the letter ;- 131 y 'dear imele. I write to say how pleased I should be if you could see your way to give up • your six glass a whisky toddy. I am sure you would find many advantages in doing so; the great- est of which Would be that, as I am persuaded, it would be a means of lengthening your days." After due interval the 'Uncle sent the following reply 1" My dear nephew. lam much obliged to you for your dutiful letter. I was so much troubled by what you said, and in particular by your kind wish I to lengthen my days, that last Friday I gave up the 'whisky. I find you're right, my boy, as to my dayi being lengthened, for, bedad, it was the longest day I ever remember." There is great trouble among the ladies who have been prominent in collecting the women's Jubilee offering. At the outset this movement received a serious check when it was announced on behalf of the Queen that she propbsed to devote its first fruits to the purchase of a replica of the Glasgow statue of the Prince Consort. But this difficulty was

wrestled with, and by patience and perseverince a very large surn has been collected. The leading spirits of the crusade were, it appears, animated by the expectation that they would be privileged per- sonally to convey their Offering, and lay it at the visible feet of Majesty. In this expectation they reckoned without the Queen, who is not uncontrol- ably fond of meeting her faithful subjects face to face„—lt has been made known that only some dozen, or at .the most a score, of ladies will be per- mitted to visit Windsor Castle as bearers of the Offering, and these will of course be selected from the titled ladies who have not done much more than lend their nameitto the,movement. It has not yet been settled what is to be done with the surplus after the statue has been paid for. The Queen will decide this, and nothing in Her Majesty's actions in connection with the Jubilee makes it safe to cherish the hope that her decision will be generally acceptable. The view set forth in this column last week on the tramway scare got up by Baron Grant has now been generally necepted. But in the meantime there has been a very serious depreciation of pro- perty, unfortunately affecting a class of the com- munity who can ill afford it. On Saturday the shares of the Tramway Company specially attacked j by Baron Grant had fallen from over twenty to IQ. ' To-day they are 18i, and will doubtless presently toucktheir old figure. But in the panic which pre- vailed last week belated shareholders literally chucked their property away- I am told that lt,raraway shares are, more than any stock, held by small tradespeople, widows, clergymen, and other sober investors. This is, however, a class peculiarly susceptible to panic, and Baron Grant is to be con- gratulated upon the skill with which he selected the field for his latest operation. There is, perhaps, nothing more striking in Lon- don than the apparently illimitable richness of the mine open to public carriers. When the under- ground railway was opened omnibus proprietors believed their last day was at hand, and were pre- pared to be ruined. To-day, there are at least three times as many 'busses plying for hire as there were before the era of the underground railway, and whilst the underground carries its tens of millions of passengers =nuttily, the omnibuses are always full. Three or four years ago, the hitherto omnipo- tent General Omnibus Company met with a rival in the London Road Car Company. This came to grief with the earliest days of the struggle, but has since been reorganised, and its traffic returns, as shown by the statements published weekly, is advancing by leaps and bounds. Yet the older com- pany not only does not suffer, but actually main- tains a steady increase of its receipts, pays its 124 per cent. dividend, and its £lOO stock is quoted at between 230 and 240. This is a prosperity in which the public fully share, for wherever the Road Car 'busses run penny fares prevail. The National Liberal club is rapidly approaching completion, and will take its part in the Jubilee celebrations. Following the example of the Reform Club, a portion of the building has been set apart for residential chambers. They will be on view from Wednesday next, and will doubtless be speed- ily snapped up. • For a man living in garcon nothing can be more convenient than to have residential chambers at his club. The situation is, of course, central, and he basall the advantagesof a splendidly appointed establishment at a cost suitable to a pri- vate purse.
THE EXA,MINER, SATURDAY. MAY 2-1, 1887.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. MEETING A,T WARRINGTON. On Thursday afternoon a meeting of the General 'Committee appointed to promote the interest of the Ship Canal locally was held in the Cocmcil Chamber, Town Hall. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) pre- sided ; and there were also present Messrs. R. A. Naylor, J. Pierpoint, Claude J. Morris, James Smethurst, J. C. Hutchings, Ernest Lees, C. Jackson Holmes, J. Geddes; Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Mr. Leigh (representing Messrs. Tunstall). In answer to a question, it was stated that shares had been subscribed for in Warrington to the value of about zomp, about £34,000 of which had been taken up through that committee. Mr. NAYLOR said they had not done quite so well lin Warrington in respect of raising 'capital as they might have done. The fact was there had been a large.atnount of opposition to the scheme on ac- count of the alteration of the route of the canal, many people being of opinion that Warrington will not receive sufficient facilities if the present plan is , carried out. He had written to several gentlemen I and otherwise communicated with them on the %lab- ject, and he had received the following letter from Alderman Davies, which weuld perhaps express the feeling of a large number of influential men of the town and district. The letter read as follows "The Old Waips,Warrington, May 24th,' 1887.—Dear Mr. Naylor,--Manchester Ship Canal—l am sur- prised our local manufacturers and authorities did' not long before now-seethe folly of making the , Warrington (I) Docks away at Wilderspool withl the London and North. Western Railway level linet between it and all the manufactories of the town., In the interest of Warrington and the canal I sub- scribed freely and worked night and day for the I scheme as it was originally proposed with the dock in the town,but it was mysteriously taken toWilders- pool. where it was useless. I was grieved to find that 1 all the work 'I had done for the town and the canal was set at nought, and I at once retired. The altered line of canal 'would not interfere with the dock being 'as you propose. In the interests,of the town and manufacturers and the canal I wig' you suc- cess, and no difficulty will rest with me, but I am sorry I cannot attend the ineeting. I am, dear Mr. Naylor, your's faithfully, Joseph Davies." The sug- gestion that he (Mr. Naylor) had to make was that they approach the Ship Canal directors to see whether they could not induce them to give War- rington another dock at the other end of the town, In addition to the one they proposed to construct in Arpley. The dock in. Arpley Meadows would be very well adapted for transhipment purposes but for the purposes of local trade it would be of yery little use. The suggestion he 'would make was this, that they present a requisition to the Ship Canal Company directors asking them to construct a cut- ting from the first lock, which they would notice from the plan would be situated in the vicinity of the Mayor's residence in Thelwall-lane, in the parish of Grappenhall. There would not be a single road to cross with this cutting, there would not be any railway in the way, and as the cutting would only be about a mile in length it would not be a very costly matter to carry out the project.. He had mentioned it to the engineer of the Ship Canal, Mr. 'Leader Williams, and he proposed or suggested that it would be the most feasible thing to take the cut Ling from above th e lock and not below it. He (Mr. Naylor) supposed that that would be due to some engineering difficulty in the way in respect of the level. The engineer appeared to look upon the proposal as a very simple matter and quite feasible and as being only a question of,cest. As to the ad- vantages to the town of the proposal he made, everybody appeared to be of one opinion that it would be of immense service. One advantage that would be gained would be that in all probability , the Midland Railway would connect the dock at Howley with their system, but as the canal was at present proposed to be carried out the London and North-Western Railway, would have a certain mono- poly. If they could get both the railways connec- ted with the canal at Warrington he thought they would agree that it would be animmense advantage ,to the trading interests generally. It had been proposed some time ago that the Che- shire Lines should make a branch to Howley Quay, and they applied for powers, and if I the directors of the Ship Canal could be persuaded to .., make the proposed cutting there could be little doubt that the Railway Company would see the advantage to themselves of making the siding. As regarded the cost in connection, with the cutting, he did not suppose it would be very large, because the river at Howley was pretty wide and deep, and it would simply require dredging, and there would be certain set offs as regarded the expense. Mr. PIRRPOINT said that if Mr. Leader Williams said Mr. Nayloes project was quite feasible, it would be simply a question as to whether the directors would advise the outlay. He spoke in favour of Mr. Naylor's proposal. Mr. NAYLOR said the present dock scheme could be modified a little. He should suggest that the whole of the land be secured for the proposed 22f acres of docks, but the construction of a portion of the docks could be deferred for a few years. In answer to a question, it was stated that the Canal Company could not alter their scheme with- out obtaining l'arliattentary powers. 'Mr. PIBRPOINT did not think that the canal direc- tors would care about interfering with their present I plans, as if they did they would again have to 'en- counter very strong opposition. It would, how- ' eVer, be a simple matter after the canal was made to arrange for the cutting suggested by Mr. Naylor. Mr. Ilirrcirmos thought it would be better to bring the 'natter for Ward before contracts were entered into. Mr. NAYLOR was also of opinion that his proposal should be brought before the directors before con- tracts were entered into. He suggested that a com- mittee should be appointed to take the matter in hand, and he understood that the canal directors were quite prepared to receive a deputation. He was sure if additional accommodation could be got from them for Warrington the application for shares wonld increase. Mr. Monum said that when the present canal scheme first came out, about two years ago, he pointed out to some of the direptors how inconveni- ent it would be to get to `the proposed docks, and . said it would be a considerable damper on the enthusiasm !of Warrington if they persisted in carrying out their plan. When the matter that had been spoken of at that meeting came out a few days ago he talked it over with two of the direc- tors. Their answer was, first that Warrington did not deserve any consideration from them because they had nothing but disappointment and cold water thrown 'upon them by the leading men of the town so far;' and, secondly, that the railway was their great difficulty as they conld not get past it conveniently. Ile told them that there was another way of doing, and that if they were to tap the traffic on the Cheshire Lines it would be absolutely necessary for thein to do something. Their answer was that if they‘in Warrington would appoint a deputation to wait upon ttiem they would arrange to have their engineer in attendance and would listen to any suggestion made to them, and say if they could do anything in the way suggested. They also said that they could not definitely fix upon any scheme, because they would have to apply to Parliament for powers to make any definite de- viation from the original plans.' , The MAYOR said it would not exactly be a devia- tion, but an addition. Mr. Iltrreirmis said there could be no question that the scheme proposed by Mr. Naylor as supple- mentary to the authorised scheme offers great ad- vantages to all works east of Warrington Bridge, and a considerable part of its cost would be saved to the Ship Canal Company by utilizing the Howley Quay warehouses and wharves for ships as well as for barges. The importance of Howley Quay as a centre of traffic is proved by the fact that at one time, so late as Monday last, there were no less than 18 barges, probably containing 1,000 tons of goods, waiting to be discharged. With such a traffic as this it was not to be wondered at that the Cheshire Lines Company were anxious to have a siding there. These considerations would doubtless carry weight with the directors to a certain extent. But in order to gain their point with them they must be pre- pared to show that their proposals were not only better for the town, but also that they could be car- ried on at less cost than the authorised scheme. Now, it must be allowed that the latter did not commend itself to those who ' ought to be most benefited by it. Hence mai4 were lukewarm, some antagonistic, and few sup- port it by becoming shareholders. The proposed dock is away from town—outside the borough— approached either by a high bridge or a level cros- sing, both very objectionable. It was also extremely costly, as beside the dock of over twenty acres, in- volving the excavation and removal of a million tons of soil, there was to be a new r'oad. These in- conveniences to the 'town and expenses to the com- pany. were necessitated by the difficulties of railway levels. Weel, ey'ry preparashun is bein' made aw o'er th' country t' mak' it a season ov grate festivity, bu' aw don't kno' so mich abeawt th' public joy. If a mon's expectin' th' bailiffs ey'ry minit throe no fawt ov his own, or if he's eawt o' wark an'.doean't kno' wheer th' next penhy 's gooin' t' cum fro', ther 'll not bi varry, mieh joy in his heart, will ther? 0, if wi cud ony create a feel& summat bike that ex- periencedbi th' slaves when they wur set free, wot / oy and hope it w'd bring to many a weary heart. f, ins tid o' tryin' to trample under foot th' liberties lov an oppressed nashun suppose wi wur to send a message ov peace an' doodwill to eawr brokken- hefted sister across th' sea, aw think at th'. harp as has hung on th' willows too lung w'd vibrate again to a new song ov thankfulness and love. , Just lately awve often yerd th' guestion axed, 6/rot kind ov a Jewbilee are yo gown' to hay?' an awre bin wonderin' wot sooart ov a Jewbilee th' mon w'd hay' at had rescued a poor family fro' th' miseries o' poverty an' -want, an' comparin' it wi th' Jewbilee ov that mon whoa bad turned a similar family adrift t' perish. Thoose little children at hay' nowt t' eat, an' whoa live in mortal dred ov thoose they shud love an' respeckt—wot a Jewbilee fur them if ther drunken fathers an' mothers re- solved t' liv' a sober life! Tawk abeaut slaves! Whoy, if wi' cud ony liberate th' drunkards fro' th' power o' drink, aw beleeov one hawve o' th' misery an' want, ud disappear fur evvur. Yo rich men whoa hay' bin blest wi' plenty o' this weed's goods, an' are lukin' eawt fur a gud investment, neaws yor toime if yo kno' ov any unfortshunate trades- man whoa's strugglin' hard t' mak' booath ends meet, an' to whom a fifty peawnd note w'd be a godsend. Sum fooake think it a grate honor t' bi presented to th' Queen, bu a far grater honor t' be able t' lift up an' save a fellow creature fro' gooin' t' ruin. Afu fifty peawnd notes distributed as above, an' wot a blessed Jewbilee booath th' receiver an' th' giver w'd experience. Th' poet says at "Kind hearts are more than coronets, an' simple faith than Nor- man blood," an' th' Maker ov Heaven. and, Earth commands at if eawr brother be waxen poor it is eawr duty to relieve him—yea, though he be a stranger.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN PARIS AT TER OPERA
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN PARIS AT TER OPERA
COMIQUE. FIFTY-SIX LIVES LOST.

Paris was alarmed on Wednesday night by a fire which broke out at the Opera Comique Theatre dur- ing the representation of the opera "Mignon." The I flames manifested themselves in the upper part of the house, which was filled with spectators of the opera. The occupants of the stalls and the parterre gained the street without any mishap, but a dread- ful panic took place among the people in the gal- leries, some of them, in sheer desperation, jumping out of the windows. The artistes rushed out of the building in their costumes. There was a number of dancers and supernumaries at the top of the theatre, and it is feared that 'Several 'of these have perished in the flames, either by suffocation or actual burning. As for the terror-stricken persons who jumped from windows, a dozen of them were seriously injured. It has now been ascertained that the fire broke out in one of the wings of the back of the stage, The flames spread rapidly along the roof, and the ceiling almost immediately fell in.- Madame Sellier, one of the dancers, perished in the flames. The firemen succeeded in reacting several persons from the upper. windows. The fire was caused by the border of one of the wings suddenly catching fire through being too close to a gas jet. Madame hferguillier was on the stage at the moment, with MM. Tasquin and Ber- nard, who on looking up perceived the flames. Five bodies terribly burnt have been conveyed from the burning building to the National Library, among them being that of a woman clasping a little boy in her arms. Two of the injured who were conveyed to a chemist's in the Rue Drouot have succumbed. the exception of Madame Sellier, the dancer, who perished in the flames, none of the actors are seriously, hurt, but the supers have suffered severely, and all those who have left the building are more or less seriously burnt. The money taken during the evening was saved and conveyed to the office of the " Gaulois," which is ,situated ;mixt door. The fire- men showed the greatest courage and devotion. M. Goblet, General Thibaudin, and M. Gragnou, the prefect of police, were on the spot since the out- break of the flames, and the officers of the military clubs on learning the news of the disaster hastened to the spot and rendered considerable assistance in the work of rescue. The artificial fire balls had ,been placed in readiness ftn. the burning of the palace at the end of the second. act, and as the supers rushed down from their places close to the roof the fire balls exploded beneath their feet. The flames spread with such rapidity that in a quarter of an hour the stage was one vast furnace, from which tongues of flames and masses of sparks rose at frequent intervals. . _ . .

div.head: PERSONAL NARRATIVE.
div.p: PERSONAL NARRATIVE.

Telegraphing on Thursday morning, a Paris cor- respondent says: The fire has now binned itself out. Mr. Sewell, solicitor to the British Embassy, who was one of the audience at the Opera Comique, has given an account of his narrow escape. He bears witness to the calmness of the audience when the alarm of fire was, given. He had been in his place in the upper tier for only. a quarter of an hour when the alarm of fire was given by one of the actors stepping forward and saying—" Mesdames et Mes- sieurs, ne bougez pas. There were then no signs of fire to be seen, but presently flakes of fire dropped down from the top of the proscenium to the stage, and volumes of stifling smoke drove the audience from their places. Mr. Sewell, with those before and behind him, made their way out of the lobby half blinded and suffocated by smoke, and the gas having been turned out, they found themselves in perfect darkness, and pursued by smoke, lit up by an occasional gleam of flame. They found their way to a window which some one had broke, and ultimately got on to a balcony at a tremendous height from the street. They could see the people it the street laying down straw and mattrasses for •theapeople to jump down upon. He saw two people jump out; but what their, fate was Mr. Sewell cannot say. _He was half stifled by the smoke that was pouring out of• the windows, and was speculating as to whether he would have to risk the jump when a move was made to the left, and it was discovered that, though interrupted by partitions, the balcony was continuous. ' Colsermertworte., Moranis—The Anglo-Turkish Con- vention signed yesterday at Constantinople stipulates that the evacuation of Egypt by the English troreps Shall take plaee at the end of three years, provided that at that time Egypt is menaced by no danger either from within or without ; that is to say, that in case of a rising like that of Arabi, or In case a an apprehended in- terference by some foreign Power, the evacuation Can- et the place. England and Turkey shall jointly.ask England Powers not to interfere in Egypt in any case. ' cmgland and Turkey further bind themselves to interfere jointly in Egypt in case of any ' t'scoble or disorder arising in that country, but r• giand reserves to herself the right to enter "'KM, should an urgent emergency require it, at the , earliest moment, without waiting for Turkey, and after notifying, to that Power her intention to act and invite ,• ,er co-operation. The Egyptian army shall be officered ol' English and Turkish officers, with a small proportion if Egyptian officers, to whom inferior grades only will given. England and Turkey engage to ask the r ewers to give their adhesion to this convention. Proto- cols annexed to the convention refer to the reforms to . be introduced in Egypt during the triennial period, and Particularly in the army and finances and the administra-, , Lion ofjustice. With regard to the finances, it is proposed . that the attributions of the caisse de /a dette which is to • oe retained shall be strictly limited to the rise and con- trol of the surrs required for the coupon, but that any attro beyond that required for that purpose shall be ap- • Dried by the Egyptian Government to any purpose they ' rsaY think proper without being subject to the control Of the officials of the cause de la dette. In other terms the Pewee of the Egyptian Government in matters of finance . should be considerably extended. as to the administra- ' tion at justice it is proposed to extend the jurisdiction ' of the mixed tribunals to criminal matters, and that foreigners shall be tried by these tribunals. IMPERIAL PARLI AMEN T.
HOUSE OF LORDS..-.MONDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took hit seat at 4 p.m. ROYAL AsstmT.—The Queen's assent was given by Royal Commission to the Duke of Connaught's Leave Act and thirty-five other Acts, many of them relating to railways and tramways. The Royal Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, the Duke of Buckingham, and the Earl of Kintore. THE TITHE RENT CHARGE BILL.

On the motion to go into Committee on the Tithe Rent Charge Bill, Lord BRABOURNE complained that the second reading was carried without discussion. Lord SALISBURY replied that he was actuated by a desire to spare their lordships an unnecsssaiy speech, and strictly followed precedent on such matters. The House then went into Committe on the bill, and several minor amendments having been adopted, the bill passed through Committee. MISCELLANEOUS.—In reply to Vincent Middleton, tle Earl of ONSLOW said that assurances had been received from the Transvaal Government that they had observed and would continue to observe the London Convention of 1884. with regard to Swaziland.--The Crofters' Hold- ings (Scotland) Bill and the County Courts Consolidation Bill wore read a third time and passed. WHITSUNTIDE RECESS. - Their lordships adjourned until the 9th Of June, and the House rose at 9 p.m.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. THE ROYAL Assiorr.—The Speaker attended the sum- mons of Black Rod to the House of Lords, where the Royal assent was given to the Duke of Connaught Leave Act, and other Acts, including the Liverpool Hydraulic Power Bill, Manchester, Middleton, and District Tram- ways Bill, West Lancashire Railway Bill, and Blackburn Corporation Tramways Bill.—The Over Darwea Cor- poration Bill was read a third time. NOTICES.—Mr. HOWELL read a long extract from the report of the Select Committee appointed to inquire into the charges of malversation against the Corporation of the City of London, and gave notice that on an early date he would move "That the conduct of the Corpora- tion is contrary to public policy, and deserves the severe condemnation of the House."—Mr.MUNDELLAintimated that on Tuesday he would bring in a bill to promote in- termediate education in Wales.—Mr. Miramar gave notice that on an early day he would move a resolution to bring home responsibility to the persons concerned in the issue of defective weapons to her Majesty's forces. In reply to Mr. Hardcastle, who complained that great inconvenience existed from an insufficient supply of small silver coin, Mr. Goscmor stated that the fault lay not with the Mint, but with the banks. On account of the extra trouble of counting and sorting, the banks pre- ferred to pay away the larger coins. Altogether there were 6,000,000 shillings and 1,680,000 sixpences ready for immediate use. .Mr. GLADSTONE asked whether the Government would arrange during the recess for the preparation and dis- tribution of a return of agrarian crime up till the end of May.—Mr. A. J. BALFOUIt promised to give the return. He was happy to add that since the Crimes Bill was introduced, a marked improvement had .sizen place in Ireland.

In answer to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. W. 11. STITTR said if it was the general wish of the House he would move at the close of the sitting the adjournment over the holi- days. so as to avoid the necessity of a meeting on Tuesday. The Government hoped to pass the second clause of the Crimes Dill before the close of the sitting.

Mr. HOARE asked the First Lord of the Treasury, in regard to the case of the Rev. J. Bell-Cox, if the Govern- ment would bring in an amending bill abolishing the penalty of imprisonment in the case of prosecutions con- cerning ritual.—Mr. CANNING had a question on the paper on the same subject.—Mr. Smrrn rejoicea that the circumstances had altered since these questions were put on the paper. Be regretted very much that impri- sonment should be inflicted as a penalty under the cir- cumstances referred to, but legislation affecting the Church had always been attended with great difficulty in this House. (Laughter.) He was not in a position to enter into any engagement orthe kind mentioned.

The remainder, he thought, might be passed over, and he expressed a hope that Clause 2 might be agreed to that evening. Mr. MARWM moved an unimportant amendment, and, after it had been discussed by Mr. M. Healy, Mr. W. H. Slurs moved "That the question be now put." For the closure 231

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY: MAY 28, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY: MAY 28, 1887.

In reply to . .4h, the ATTOWSZY•GENEMAT. said there were _4 44peal cases before the House of Lords awaiting judgment. One was heard in April last, two in August last, and eight during the sittings of the present year. In many cases points of law had arisen. In answer to Mr. Bradlaugh, Sir J. Goasv said the terms under which the ruby mines in Burmah were to be worked were still under consideration. In answer to Mr. T. O'Connor, Colonel KING-HARMAN said the Chief Secretary had received the letter of Mr. Patrick Egan of April gBth last, but it was impossible to make any conditions for the return of Mr. Egan to Ireland.
THE COMMIS.,SION ON WARLIKE STORE.-IMPORTANT BFPORT.

The report of the Royal Curr.mission appointed to inquire into the system under which patterns of warirke stores are adopted. and the stores obtained and passel for her Majesty's service, was issued on Monday. The commissioners remark that they experienced some difficulty in deciding practically upon the limits of inquiry. The radiest difficulty arose upon the exami- nation of their first witness' Mr. Smith, then Secretary for War.—The Chairman of the commission (Sir James Stephen) strongly held the opinion that the powers of the Secretary of State not only formed a part of the system under which warlike szeres were provided for the public service, but were the leading and most essential part of it. Mr. Smith admitted that the Commission ought to deal with those points in general, but was decidedly of opinion it ought' not to inquire Into the general ad- ministration of the Ordnance Department for the last feiv years, and more particularly into the q uesfion whether the reserves of stores had been kept up to their proper height The comm issioners accordingly treated as confiden tial such official reports bearing upon this question as have come to their knowledge; but thcy thought they were not only entitled but bound to ascertain as completely as they could the general nature of the powers of the Secretary of State, and to epxress their opinion on them. Analagous difficulties arose regarding the special part of their inquiry.— that into the complaints made since July, 1881, as to warlike stores. The most important of the complaints were that systematic fraud and corruption took place between the years 1858 and 1863, that the administra- tion of the Ordnance Department has ever since been conducted more or less under the influence of that fraud and • corcuption, and that the particular results finally arrived at cannot be fully understood or fairly criticised unless this is borne in min.]. After describing the general system of the Ordnance De- partment, the Commissioners find that the great defects of the existing system are three. First, it has no definite obits& ; second, it has no efficient head; and third, it has no properly organised method of dealing with technical questions which arise as to the purchase or construction of warlike stores. In other words, it requires more system, more puplicity, more vigour in administration, and more special knowledge in council." The Commissioners add Our first and most important recommendations are aimed at the removal of these defects by means which would both facilitate the Parliamentary discussion of these subjects and increase the stringency of Parliamentary control over miiitary expenditure. The first step to be taken is to establish a definite standard, according to which military administration ought to be regulated, and at the attainment of which it ought to aim. The establish- ment of such a standard would have to apply to other subjects than stores, because the different parts of our military and naval system have a relation to each other, and it is impossible to say precisely what should be done with regard to any one of them, unless it i. known 'what is to be done with regard to the rest." The Commissioners further suggest that an account of the actually existing State of our armaments might be made out every year, and would show distinctly how the country stood; aid that technical questions ought to be from time to time considered and solemnly decided upon by some duly qualified body. This would not only fa 't intelli- gent Parliamentary discussion of the matter, but would form a guide to public opinion, and give a strong security to the piaMic in general that their money isms being intelligently applied to the purposes for which it was intended. The contention that such publicity would involie the danger of giving information to enemies, might have weight if secrecy were possible: but it was not. The Commissioners goon to recommend a readjustment of the duties of the Secretary for Wjr, with the Ordnance Department, the reorganisation of the Ordnance Department itself, and the ascertainment of the objects at which the Ordnance Department, as re-Jo organised, shall aim.
SCOTCH AND IRISH GRIEVANCES.---THE STATE OF BUSINESS. • _ _

_ Mr. W. H. Swim having moved that the House at its rising adjourn, to Monday, the 6th June, Dr. CLARK called attention' to the administration of the Crofters' Act in regard to loans to fishermen authorised by that measure.. He complained of the harsh terms that were exacted, and then called attention to the desirability of inquiring into the condition of shepherds, ploughmen, farm servants, cotters. and other agriculturist labourers of Scotland, especially in reference to the system of service, hours of labour, housing, and the physical and moral results of the bethy system. Mr. ANDERSON asked the Government to introduce a measure to enable the Scotch peasants to obtain small patches of land compulsorily. Mr. QUILTER called attention to the injury done to tradespeople by the arrangements made in a number of gaols for the manufacture of certain articles of commerce. _ _
Mr. 8. SMITH called attention to the paucity of Non- conformist magistrates in Flintshire in propoTtion to the Nonconformist population. Mr. OSBORN MORGAN endorsed the complaint. _

Mn STUART Woartgr, replying to Mr. Ziuilter, said he could not admit that in the contracts made by the Govdrnment In reference to prison labour there was any departure from the pledges given to the House as to the avoidance of competition in ordinary trade. Mr. Picrox called attention to the growing infliction of disease on the people of the United Kingdom under the Compulsory Vaccination laws, and was proceecr •,e to discuss the question at some length when he was called to order by the Speaker, who pointed out that he was Infringing a rule of the House by arguing a matter as to which he had a specific notice on the paper for a future day. Mr. RITOIIII, on behalf of the Local Government Board, asserted the duty of the Government to see that the law as to vaccination was carried out, and, while promising his personal attention to all legitimate complaints., said he could not promise that the Government would insti- tute any general inquiry into the subject. Mr. T. M. FIFALT objected to the constitution of the Irish Court of Appeal, and complained that Lord Ash. bourne should be now sitting in Ireland to decide cases under the Land Act of which he was so bitter an opponent. The hon. gentleman also suggested that it. would be better for Lord Ashbourne to follow the example of the English Lord Chancellor and refrain from sitting in the Court of Appeal. While the hon. gentleman was referring to the action of the Irish 'Lord Chancellor in the Kelly case, he was interrupted by Mr. ATIC/NSON, who rose to order, on the ground that Mr. Healy was putting a nonsensical contention before the House.

The SPEAKER, interposing, declared that the expression " nonsensical " was unparliamentary. Mr. ATKINSON withdrew the expression. Mr. HEALY concluded his speech by warning the Government to beware of the effect of their action in this and other matters on the public mind in Ireland. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND justified the notion of the Lord Chaneellor of Ireland, who, he said, had always exercised the most extensive jurisdiction in cases of appeal. • Mr. E. ROBERTSON (Dundee) called attention to the extraordinary situation in which the House was placed In regard to the general business of the country. So far they had passed two clauses of the Crimes Bill, and the I Duke of Connaught'a Leave Bill, and the country re- garded with disapproval and disappointment the small mutts achieved. (Ministerial and counter cheers.) The Government, he contended, had led to this failure of fruitful legislation by their disastrous Irish policy, which had been ill-conceived and obstinately defended. More- over, having undertaken the tremendous policy they had initiated, they had failed to adopt the proper means to carry it through the closure resolution they had obtained, having been so overweighted with the 200 majority that the Speaker and Chairman held that it was unworkable. (Opposition cheers.) Beyond this, he accused the Government of attempting to make party capital out of the state of things they had them- selves brought about, assisted by an alliance with an illegitimate Opposition. (Opposition cheers.) As ai final charge against the Government, he asserted that they were also using the existing state of public busi- ness as a means, not only of attack on the Liberal pasty, but also of exalting the House of Lords by disparaging the House of Commons. Lord Salisbury never made a speech without making party capital out of the deadlock caused by his own Godernraent, and he (Mr. Bobertson) was surprised that the leader of that House should sit silent when such charges were made against an assembly it was his duty to protect. (Opposition cheers.) Sir Witrittn LAWSON congratulated the right hon. i gentleman on the motion for adjournment, the best he could make, though somewhat extraordinary in the face of the statement that for the preservation of law and order coercion was a matter of the first necessity. (Hear, hear.) It had since been made manifest that the action of the Government was merely on behalf of some MO gentlemen suffering from boycotting, and yet the leader of the House deserted them. (Hear, hear.) With the strongest, most loyal majority a Government ever had, backed up bye servile con ti n gen tof supporters,the Govern- ment were yet. willing to adjourn fora fortnight, and leave law and order in Ireland to crumble to atoms. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It disclosed the utterly sham character of the Government 'policy—(near, hear),—but he rejoiced at the prospect of the holiday, for time would be given for the great Liberal party to go to the country and instruct the people on what had taken place, whence they would return to the House like giants refreshed with new wine—(laughter),—strengthened, more deter- mined than ever, to continue most persistent and most determined opposition to what he characterised as the most unjust, most unconstitutional, and unnecessary measure ever introduced to a legislative assuribly. (Cheers.) Mr. DILLON having controverted the contention of the , Irish Attorney• General as to the action of the Irish Lord Chancellor,
Mr. W. H. &urn appealed to the House to allow the motion as to adjournment for the holidays to be put, and the motion being at once put was agreed to.

THE LONDON CORPORATION SCANDAL. Mr. BRADLAUGH gave notice that on Tuesday, June 28th, he would move the resolution standing in his name as to the charge of malversation against the London Cor- poration. Mr. E. Roanirrson (Dundee) give notice that that day five weeks he would move the resolution condemning the representation of Universities. The House adjourned at 6 15 until the 6th June..

RELEASE OF THE REV. J. BELL-COX. The official authority for the release of thel Rev. Jas. Bell-Cox did not reach Walton Gaol, Liverpool, till 11 o'clock on Saturday, by which time the rev. gentleman's friends, who had assembled at an early hour, had dis- persed. Mr. Bell-Cox, who was anxiously awaiting the arrival of the missive, at once deft the gaol, and drove home unaccompanied. A very large congregation assem- bled at St. Margaret's, Liverpool, on Sunday morning, in anticipation of the appearance of the Rev. J. 13e114x, whose release from Kirkdale Prison on Saturday was a source of satisfaction to the whole of the church. The rev. gentleman attended the morning service; but beyond announcing the hymns took no part in the cele- brations. The officiating miniat'er was the curate, Mr. 'Payne, and the sermon was preached by the Rev. Mr. Wainwright, of London Docks. The ceremonial was in all points as high as usual. Before the sermon a brief request was uttered by Mr. Bell-Cox to "return thanks to God Almighty for His great mercy vouchsafed to us:" but no other word was uttered in rvference to the recent imprisonment, the service proceeding in ..11 respects as though the lamentable occurrence had never happened. It is stated on authority that this is the course Mr. Bell. Cox has decided scrupulously to adhere to. Mr. Bell- Cox hopes to bh able to leave Liverpool for an extended holiday, as the strain of the past months has been very considerable and has told upon his health. Sir P. Heywood presided at a meeting held at Derby, on Mc iday night, to protest against the recent imprisonment of the ReV. J. Bell-Cox. Canon Knox Little was one of the spettkers, and said Mr. Cox had stood out under most difficult cir- cumstances for great principles. He believed the day would come when the historian would honour the names of Dale, Enraght, Green, and Cox as of men who wecre so law-abiding that they would not break the law of the Church and realm in favour of the law of the realm alone.

The ironworkers on sirike at Bolton have rejected a proposal to retnain at work three months, withdraw the objections to overtime, and then, should they desire a third party to be called in, the ,masters will agree,to the mayoricting as referee on the question of the proposed increase. _

Lily Fairhurst and Mary Bannister were on Monday committed for trial by the Manchester stipendiary on a charge of fraud. Prisoners kept a bogus registry office, and advertised for domestic servants. A large number of girls applied, and paid the fees demanded, but in no case did they obtain a situation. Complaint was made to the police authorities, and inquiries instituted showed that the prisoners had carried out the fraud on a most extensive scale.

THE STRIKE AT BOLTON.—On Tuesday night an attack wail made upon the foundry ef Messrs. J. and E. Wood, of Bolton, where a number of workmen from Scotland were lodged, and were eupplying plsces vacated by the ordinary workmen going out on strike. The windows of the foundry were smashed, and other damage was done. On Wednesday morning, upon the gates of the factory being opened, the Scotchthen marched oat and proceeded to the rendizvous of the members of the Strike Committee. After an intorview the men left for Scotland, assuring their brethren on strike that they bad been brought to Bolton without any knsw- ledge that there was a dispute lu the trade.

1 • • About 1,200 weavers in the cast end Of Glasgow have , struck work for an advance of 10 per cent, in their wages. , The Rev. Dr. Geo. Jeffrey, clerk of the Glasgow United Presbyterian Presbytery, and e::-runderntor of tic Synod, died on Monday. , A monument to the Marquess of Montrose, "the great Marquess," is to be placed in St. Giles's Cathedral, chiefly by gentlemen of the Clan Graham. Dr. Rowland Anderson has furnished the design, the carrying out of which will cost about £l,OOO. In consequence of the reduction of 4d. per pound on the rate of duty on unmanufactured tobacco, which took effect on Saturday, the supplies taken out of bond during the past two weeks have fallen considerably be- low the average. A Scotch correspondent sends particulars of the con- dition of the grouse on the moors in the North. The reports are generally cf a very favourable character, and it is stated that there is no ground for the rumours wnich have got abroad of disease among the birds. A Devonshire gentleman, conceiving that the wearing of the Queen's favourite flower would form an interest- ing feature in the forthcoming celebration of Her Majesty's Jubilee, communicated With General Ponsonby, who informed him that the letter had been placed before the Queen, and that Her Majesty's favourite flower in the summer was the rose. We live In the time of high prices. An absurdly extrava- gant price was given the other day for a new variety of orchid. The other day an offer of £20,000 for that good old horse Bendigo was refused. On Saturday a pony, which was described as the best living animal of its class, was sold at the Olympia Horse Show, and the lucky purchaser believes that he will be able to get very nearly four' figures for it. . DEPARTURE or MORMONS—On Saturday the Guion steamer Nevada left the Mersey for New York. Amongst her passengers `were 200 Mormons, bound for Salt Lake City, Utah, to join the Mormon community in that place. The chief towns in England from which the Mormons who sailed on Saturday were collected, are London,New- castle, Manchester, Bristol, and Liverpool. There were also some from Glasgow and Soutb Wales. , Renecnoe or Sires Ceorreas' Reives.—The Crofter Commissioners have given their decision in the first cases of application by Skye crofter tenants for a reduction of rent. On Lord Macdonald's estate rents have been re- duced on an average of 25 per cent, and on Colonel Fraser's Kilmuir estate the reductiop is 33i per cent. In these eases very large sums owing as arrears were I entirely cancelled by the Commissioners. STEALING • BATTALION'S PAT.—AS the 3rd Battalion of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers was about to be paid off on I Saturday morning, after their month's annual training, ' one of the officers' servants, named Kelly, absconded with £l2O. He obtained the money by sending a note to the officers' mess, asking for it as the men were waiting, and • by an accident he unfortunately received it He got clear away, and the police have not yet succeeded in tracing him. Arreater TO Wriecx KW OVERSEER'S RESIDENCE. —At about one a.m. on Saturday last, Mr. Hardy, assistant-overseer of the Hebburn collieries; was awakened by a loud report, and found that one of the windows of his house had been shattered by an explo- sion. He informed the police of the occurrence, who discovered the remains of a three-gill bottle, which had evidently been filled with powder, and placed on the window-sill. The affair has caused much excitement, as 1 a similar outrage,took place recently. I THE BANERUPTCT OF LORD COLIN CAMPBELL.-- In the London Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, Mr. Registrar Giffard made a receiving order against the estate of Lord Colin Campbell, of 2, Bryanston-square . The petitioning creditor is the Duke of Marlborough, whose claim of £971 isin respect of taxed costs incurred , . in the Cohn Campbell divorce suit. Neither the debtor, I nor anyone on his behalf, appeared when the case was I called on. Mr. George Lewis was for the petitioning . creditnn—Two of the principal creditors, in addition to i the Duke of Marlborough, are stated to be Lady Colin 1 Campbell and Captain Shaw. COTTONSEED OIL ANN BUTTERINE.—TWO-tiliidS of the cottonseed oil sold in the 'States goes to`the makers of lard and butterine; and its use to the extent of about 20 per cent. has, it is stated, been one of the most powerful influences in reducing the price of lard. It is also being used for cooking, and a large proportion of the oil taken • with salads and sardines IS the product of the cotton fields. Scientific men declare that it is perfectly whole- some, and some even say that it is better than animal fats. It is estimated that not far from 600,000 tons of cottonseed are used in this industry every year, and that. • from 400,000 to 500,000 barrels of crude oil are produced, half of which is exported from the States. 1 1 THE EDUCATION OF TEACHERS.—A deputation from the 1 Education Reform League waited upon the Vice-Presi- dent of the Council on Saturday to urge the importance ' of the University education of teachers. Professor Stuart, M.P., introduced the deputation, which included the Marquis of Ripon, Sir Lyon Playfair, and several representatives of colleges. Sir William Hart-Dyke, in replying, said that, as there was a Commission now sit- ting on education he could not make any lengthened remarks. He cordially sympathised with their object, bid was unable to give any pledges as to details. Allud- ing to the formation of the Education League, he begged them not to allow it to drift into a political association. Tim KENTISH TOWN MURDER.—ARRESTS AT ROCH- 1 DALE.—The Rochdale police arrested some days ago two of a party of four men who were loitering about shops in that town with a presumably felonious intention. Their companions, who had a conveyance in readiness 'for flight, were apprehended later on at Oldham, where they had been concerned in several shop robberies. In- quiries by the Rochdale authorities created a belief that their two prisoners ivere concerned in the murder of Mrs. Samuels in .Kentish Town, last March: but., on Monday, I when they appeared in the dock, they could not be identified by witnesses from London. One of them, how- ever, was recognised as a convicted thief named Daly, and he was further remanded.' His companion, who calls himself Smith, was handed over to the Oldham ; police. MANOMETAN LADIES IN EVENING DEM.—It is an open secret that at a dinner lie gave to a circle of friends a few evenings ago, at the Bristol Hotel, the ex-Khedive of Egypt (Ismail Paaha), his Highness's third wife, as well as the wife of Ibrahim Bey, his physician, were present in the evening dress prescribed by European fashion. Afterwards the ex-Khedive, with his third wife and suite, paid a visit to one of the theatres. This is, of course, in direct violation of the tradition which forbids a Mahornetan lady to hold any converse whatever with even the most intimate of the male friends of her hus- band, and which prescribes the use of the yashmak, or thick veil, whist' conceals everything but the eyes of the wearer. In the precedent thus established there may be the beginning of an improvement in the position of Oriental women in the not remote future. BELLE VUE GAOL.—The Prison Commissioners have decided on the abolition of Belle Vue Gaol, Manchester, and the building will shortly be pulled down. For some time past the prisoners have been gradually drafted away to linutsford—whete the large accommodation has been hitherto only partially used--Strangeways, and elsewhere in the county. The transfer will shortly be fully accomplished. The warders and officers are also !Incline situations elsewhere. Belle Vue has within recent years been regarded SS almost a model geol. In the government reports it has been spoken of very highly on account of the excellent discipline maintained, the useful work done by the prisoners in brush-making and the like, and the small amount of punishment which has been necessary. The reasons for the demolition of the building are, we understand, imperative. . A Hooe lkser.—The great blast at Llanberis, North Wales, for which preparations have been in progress for the past three years, took place at one o'clock on Satur- day. and was completely successful. About two tons of "gelatine," equal in strength to nineteen tons of powder, were used, the object, being to effect a displacement of ninety to a hundred thousand tons of bad rock at Dinor- wic Slate Quarry, which made it dangerous for the men to work about it. Either the displacement had to be effected, or the men must cease work, whereas now there will be means of employment furnished for many more men. Notices were posted in Llanberis requesting the people to leave their houses, and to leave their doors and 'windows open. This was done, and, with trifling excep- tions, the after effects were harmless. The explosion was fired by electricity, and the shock was followed by a terrible report, the entire mass being lifted up and toppled over into the \Victoria section of the quarry. Traffic was stopped in the locality, and there was an immense gathering posted around to witness this—the heaviest, most costly, and most. effective explosion ever caused in the quarry districts of Wales. SUICIDE OF A WIpAN MAN THROUGH LOTE.—The Cheshire coroner investigated a sad case of suicide on Saturday, at Brooklands. Oliver Gerrard, a labourer, lately em- ployed at the Manchester Exhibition buildings, threw himself into a pool of water at Brooklands and drowned ' himself, through a love affair.—James Gerrard, brother . of the deceased, said he last saw the deceased at Old ' Trafford, when he told him he was going down to see • his young lady at Sale, apd if they did not put things ! eight he would "bottom some water before long." ' Witness told him not to be so foolish, and he went away.—George Fisher,' foreman in the yard .of the . Brooklands Hotel, said that the deceased went there about half-past nine on Wednesday evening, and gave him a silver watch to be forwarded to his brother. He did not apnear strange, but was very thought- ' eel.—Emily Long, the young woman I to whom Gerrard was engaged, said they were to have been mar- ried in Whit-week. On Wednesday 'night she saw him at her sister's house in Sale, and left him without saying "Good night." His sister-in-law had tried to set him against her, and some unpleasantness had resulted. Be \ did not say he would drown himself, but he told her on • the previous Sunday night that if she did not have him . he would take care nobody else had. The police having ; given evidence as to the finding of the body in the pit, the Coroner said it was a very lamentable case. There seemed to have been some busy-body who had meddled and brought the young man to the verge of despair. He seem to have felt acutely his position, and gone and de- stroyed himself. A verdict of suicide during temporary insanity was returned. Thedeceased was a fine athletic ,young fellow, and was 24 years ef age. Hewes a native . of Wigan.

div.head: BURNLEY AND THE SHIP CANAL
div.p: BURNLEY AND THE SHIP CANAL

On Monday, at the Mechanise' Institution, Burnley, a meeting called by requisition, and presided over by the Mayor%(Alderman Keighley), was held for the pur- pose of assisting the company in raising the required capital for the Manchester Ship Canal scheme. Besides the Mayor there were on the platform Mr. Jas. E. Platt, director. Mr. Leader-Williams, engineer, and Mr. Bostiin T. Leach, Mr. Rawlinson, J.P., Alderman Baron, J.P., Councillors Flouldsworth, Proctor, Lancaster, Burrows, C. M. Foden, Mr. N. P. Gray. There was a large attend- ance. A large sketch of the Canal—being a plan of the model on view at the Royal Jubilee Exhibition, Manches- ter—and comparative sections of Continental ship canals were hung on the walls. The Mayon said the canal would shorten the time and lessen the expense in geting goods to and from Burnley. The canal would be of great benefit to Burnley. It would lower the rate of goods manufactured at Burnley which had to be shipped direct at, lea.st from 601. tole. per ton. To people who had a large traffic ss. or 6s. a ton vnts a handsome income.

Mr. Jamv.s Ptarr said the company wished to havethe support of all Lancashire towns in their efforts to com- plete the scheme. In the district which comprised Blackburn. Burnley, and Preston there existed perhaps the largest number of looms collectively of any part of the world; in fact, most of the loom trade of England was comprised in that area. The capital invested in trade in that district WHS. about £14,000,000. There were in Lancashire 42,000,000 spindles and 470,000 looms. The length of the canal was about 35 miles. Ships would be able to bring raw cotton to Manchester, and take the manufactured goods from Manchester, at a much cheaper rate than that charged by the railway corn- Panies• For instance, the people of Blackburn would save about £13,000 per anninn on the ex- portation of their cOtton goods from Manchester. He did not think Mandester and Oldham, and the sun. roundthg towns should do everything in the matter, but he thought all the towns which would benefit by the canal should help them. He had heard a rumour that the Burnley people were rather against the canal because they were under the impression that large cotton mills would be put up all along the canal side, and would take the trade from Burnley. That was a stupid idea. Such a avelopment Would take very many years, if it took place at all. A few ironworks would crop up along the canal side, but that would take many years. He did not see why the trade that came across the Atlantic should not come up to Manchester, and if that was accomplished they must bear in mind that they would get the sea about 30 miles nearer Burnley, which would be a very great advantage. (Cheers.) Mr. LEADER-WILLIAMS, before describing and illustrat- ing the eketch, observed that the Manchester Ship Canal was a scheme of which he was proud to be the engineer. Competition was becoming so severe with foreign countries, who had constructed ship canalg, that unless this country secured every possible advantage • they would lose the race He pointed out the course of the canal which he said was tidal as far as Latchford locks; and there was as much trade at Warrington to justify a ship canal to that point. The essence of the success of the scheme was in the fact that there WAS TIO wear and tear in the water, and when the trade doubled the ex- pense did not necessarily increase. Mr. T. LEACH, in a brief address, pointed out how the trade of the interior was embarrassed and burdened by heavy railway rate& and besides that they had a keener foreign competition than ever they had had before. They were able to bring iron from Belgium to London at ss. per ton, while It cost them 12s. per ton to take it from Chesterfield ; and all other kinds of goods were in the same position, The Leeds and Liverpool Canal had been paying between 18 to 25 per cent, being a three or four times better average than their best railways. It was not a bubble scheme, but headed by some of,their best Manchester merchants The present directors and their friends had invested nearly £200,000, and the Consulta- tive Committee had invested about £lOO,OOO. Councillor LAticasrait moved the following resolu- tion ;-6*That this [abating congratulates the directors of the Manchester, Ship Canal on the success which is attending their efforts to raise half of the required capi- tal locally, and pledges itself to assist them in obtaining a total sum of at least £4,000,000 in the district." The scheme was one which must affect Burnley indirectly in a very important manner. It was for all to try and do something—to take a few shares—to help on the great enterprise. (Hear, hear.) Mr. N. P. GRAY, J. P., seconded, and believed the scheme would be an instrument of great good to Lancashire trade.

Mr. J. RAIVLIN3the -supported the itil,tion, and said he had the pleasure of giving evidence before the Com- mittees of the Houses of Lords and Commons in favour of the canal, and he tried to slow in what way the canal would benefit the trade of North-East Lancashire. He WM bound to any that one of the principal things that made him so convinced that the canal would be a suc- cess, svhs the determined oPposition that. was given to it by'intetested parties in Liverpool. The. Liverpool Cor- poration and the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board gave it the most determined Opposition that any bill had ever received He did not think • the canal would injure Liverpoolwbut he thought it would bring about such a great increase of trade that both Liverpool and Man- chester would be benefited. He hoped the Butnley people would give it all possible support. • ; The motion was then put, and carried with applause. Alderman BACON proposed, and Mr. DOCKETT seconded, a vote of thanks to the MAYOR, who responded, and thought that all the adults of Burnley might raise a share each. In that manner they would raise about 10,000 shares, and bethought lt Would be in the interests of the town if clubs were formed for the collection of subscrip- tions. Ho also remarked that no ship canal had ever been made which had not paid, and no one bad everbeen made which had not developed the trade of the district. The workpeople at Messrs. Platt's mills, Oldham' had taken up 5,000 shares, and he thought this ought to be an example to the working-men of Burnley.

It is a fact worthy of note that no less than five or six managers of provincial theatres are mayors of the boroughs in which their playhouses stand. The Mayor of Cambridge controls the destinies of the theatres in both his own and the sister University City of Oxford. THE Fagg CHURCH OF SCOTLAND.—The Free Church Assembly sitting in. Edinburgh on Monday, adopted, by 322 votes against 66, a resolution declining to engage in negotiations with the Established Church on the question of reunion whilst the matters of Establishment and endowment were excluded from discussion.

HOLIDAY R‘'FLECTIONS —With the approach of 11 hitsun- tide the mind seems naturally to turn to anticipations of Swiss climbing and Rhine experiences, the remembrances of which go so far to make the remainder of our En dish year bearable. Talking of the Rhine, one of, perhaps, the most pleasant experiences to the traveller is—next to the contrast in the scenery—the change in the style of living, which hie 'holiday there introduces him to. Take the matter of wine I alone. How his knowledge of that article seems to be mud denly enlarged by the light refreshing bottle of Huchheirner !which he gets—say at St Goar or Coblentz—and which he 1 mentally resolves, shill, in future, appear on his table at home. Circumstances, have, it 5 true, hitherto prevented the realization of this resolution, but in future, the new scheme of Messrs. W. and &. Gilbey, for supplying the light table wines of Germany anti Hungary—Hoch heimer and Karlowitz—at One Shilling per bottle, should do much to meet what is a rapidly growing demand.—The .Iforning :Pest, 21st May, 1887.

little he knew as Secretary of State for War. Mr. SMITH is not, of course, alone in having occupied this peculiar position, and equally, of course, the Commissioners do not blame the individual, but the system. " The office of Secretary of State for War," says the Report, "being one which for its full dis- charge would require a great amount of mili- tary and technical knowledge, has for a num- ber of years been in the hands of persons who are entirely destitute of both. In these circumstances, it is obvious that the Secretary of State must rely upon his subordinates, and these are numerous, are not generally known to the public, and are protected from all responsibility by the position in which they stand. . . . The effect of this is in the first place that there is no definite respon- sibility whatever, and in the second place there is no continuity in the policy of the office." In other words there is mismanagement and inefficiency resulting in swords that cannot be trusted, bayonets that bend, and cartridges that jam The position of the Surveyor General of Ordnance would seem to be just as misatisfactory, for the report adds—" the inherent weakness of the Secretary of State is increased by the inherent weakness of his principal subordinate, the Surveyor-General of the Ordnance." Two weak bases cannot, of course, make one strong one, and as things stand John Bull need not wonder that he gets so little for the large sum that he spends annually on *the Army and Navy. The Commissioners go into various details, and make various recommend- ations, the principal of which is that the office of Master-General of Ordnance should be revived, and that it should be held by a thoroughly competent man who should be independent of party changes. What is ob- viously wanted is a working chief who under- stands the machinery of war from end to end, and who can be held responsible to Parlia- ment when things go wrong. It is very in- convenient when, as at present, the whole machinery is out of gear, and there is nobody who can be blamed. If we were only in a position at the present moment to solemnly try and carefully hang a Chief Secretary or a Surveyor. General—what a wholesome effect it would have on subordinate officials! It would be quite a healthy operation.

AT Runcorn, there has been a conflict be- tween the Police Authorities and the Com- missioners, and, for the moment the police have got the worst of it. It seems that a number of persons who have stalls in Bridge-street, in front of the Market Hall, are regarded by the police as obstructors of the highway, and on Monday they were brought before the Magistrates on a charge of ob- structing the street. Seeing that the stall- holders had paid for the right to do business in the space allotted to them, it was natural that they should look to the Commissioners to defend them.; and in this they were not dis- appointed. The Law Clerk, Mr. W. H. LINAKER, undertook the defence, and con- tended that the Magistrates had no jurisdic- tion. He urged that, before the Market Hall was built in 1-853, the Market was held in Bridge street, and as the Market Hall had not been sufficient to meet the require- ments of the stallholders. the Commissioners had all along exercised their right to let stalls in Bridge-street as heretofore. Superinten- dent HOLLINGWORTH, on the other hand, alleged that the road had become dedicated to the public, and that it was the duty of the Police Authorities to .keep it free from ob- struction. Evidence was given to the effect , that there was plenty of room in the Market Hall, and that Bridge-street was incon- veniently‘ crowded; but, after hearing the cases at some length,the Bench dismissed the summonses on the ground that the Magis- trates had no jurisdiction. Superintendent HOLLINGWORTH, who stated that he was acting under the instructions of the CHIEF CONSTABLE of the county, intimated that he should appeal against the decision; and it may thus happen that a good deal of time and money may be wasted over a case, which, as it seems to us, ought not—at this stage at any rate—to have come in court. The police are undoubtedly custo- dians of highways, and it is their duty in the interests of the public to see that they are kept free from obstruction. But in a case of this kind, where a large issue is involved; and where the real offenders—if thele be an of- fence—are a lima of Commissioners, it is certainly undesirable to resort to law until the ordinary means 'have been tried which ordinary courtesy suggests. . ,If ,Runcorn, instead of being governed by Commissioners, had been a borough, it would in all proba- bility have had its borough police, who would have been-unable to act in a case of this kind, for it is not likely that they would betinstrncted to take proceedings against their own masters. it is an accident of the situation that the Runcorn police are not under the control of the Runcorn authorities; and this being so it is hardly wise to take ad- vantage of that accident—until other means have failed—to force a public conflict-between two public bodies. The police have taken action, and they have failed, and the imme- @late effect is that they have weakened their own authority. Even granting that they are right in the view they take that Bridge-street is obstructed—an d it cannot be questioned that some obstruct ion is caused—the 'better way of dealing vith the grievance would have been to bring the matter before the Commissioners with an appeal to them to remedy an objectionable state of things. If the Commissioners, disregarding such an appeal, thought fit to stand simply upon their legal right, it would then have been soon enough to carry the matter into a court of law. It is not too late, we hope, even now to suspend hostilities, and resort to some- thing in the nature of comeiliation and arlyi- tration. Let Bridge-street be kept free from obstruction; but surely that can be arranged without appealing to an alien authority. Home Rule' even in a matter of this kind, is better than Coercion.

The members of the House of Commons have been dismissed for the Whitsuntide holidays alter struggling through two clauses of the Coercion Bill. This represents the sum total of the business done, and it is bad at the best. Members of Parliament, whether Iristror English, who believe, as Lord SALIS- BURY said of the Crimes Bill, that the Coer- cion Bill is calculated to creatg ten times as much mischief as it will repress, are doing no more than their duty in resisting its pas- sage through Parliament to the utmost of their power. Small as has been the progress made with regard to the measure, something has been done towards softening some of its most villanous features; and this is the answer that is to be made to !hose who talk randomly about obstruction. There is no discussion of the bill, so far as the supporters of the Go- vernment are concerned. It is left to the Oppositica, and the word has gone forth that

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 28. 1887
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 28. 1887

the Opposition are to be coerced into passing the Coercion Bill. After clamouring wildly against a mild form of closure, the Tories are just as wildly applying the most stringent closure they have been able to frame. When Mr. GLADSTONE requested that some steps should be taken to give the House better con- trol of its business, the members who consti- tute the present Administration were loud in their denunciation of what they called an attempt to gag the House of Commons. Liberty of speech was a sacred thing, and must be preserved at all hazards. They knew, of course, how absurd it was to suggest that Mr. GLADSTONE would interfere with reason- able discussion ; but it was regarded as "a j good cry" to talk about the gag. Mr. GLAD- STONE'S Rules of Procedure were passed, the world moved on, and nobody was injured. The Tories who had protested so much came into office, and after a brief spell of work, they expressed themselves as dissatisfied with the new Rules of Procedure. Did they want to relax them? Not a bit of it. With the ' brazen impudence which so often character- ises them, they threw to the winds all their talk about interfering with liberty of speech, and insisted on a gag—a real gag—a gag that could be applied, ay, even in the middle of a member's speech. They have got the gag, and the use that is being made of it is as brutally frank and direct as is the sting of a wasp. Mr. SMITH will be known in history not as a heaven -born minister, but as an earth- born gagger. He is like a child with a new toy ; he brings it to the frcnt at the most un- seasonable time, and in the most unseason- able way. He is like a child, too, in not fully understanding his toy, and in handling it clumsily. There was an all-night silting on Monday night—the House did not rise till half-past five on Tuesday morning—and Mr. SMITH applied his gag again and again. But he made a mull of it at times, for Mr. MAURICE HEALY was twice succQssful in ap- pealing to the Chair when the leader of the House of Commons was breaking his own Rules. That the Government were in a false , position in prolonging the sitting is shown by the fact that they were driven by sheer stress of argument to accept many of the amendments of the Irish members, and by their being compelled to give up the sub- section by which it was proposed to revive the monstrous provisions of the " Whiteboy" Acts. The Coercion Bill is not yet passed, and we trust that the Opposition will, after the holidays, return to the House of Com- mons renewed in health and strength, and ready to fight it at every stage in the bare hnpe that by some happy accident it may perish before it stains the statute book of the United Kingdom. •

The Tithes Bill has passed through Com- mittee in the House of Lords; and as it leaves their lordships it is just such a measure as might be expected of them. It is a choice bit of class legislation. It is no relief whatever to the over-burdened farmer: fm, instead of payine: the parson cirect he is asked to pay tithes to his landlord. It will certainly please the clergy ; it is a relief to them and to no one else, for it makes them cock-sure of their money —be the seasons what they may. The farmers must be very slow and very stupid it they allow themselves to be bamboozled by the Tithes Bill.

The "Daily News" says—" A deputation, representing the iron trade of Great Britain, waited upon Sir Henry Holland at the House of Commons, on Monday, to urge the Government to take action against the proposed increase of Canadian imporf duties on metals. The proceedings were private, but it is understood that the Colonial Sec- retary declared himself unable to give a favourable answer." This must be pleasant news for the Tory Reciprocitarians. They promised great things in matters of trade, if the country would only give the Tories a chance. The chance was given, the oc- casion has arisen, and the Tories are, as usual, helpless.

It is a shameful breach of the law that, in consequence of the bungling of the Runcorn Guardians, or School Board, or both, child- ren are being kept from school through -lack of provision for paying school fees when he parents are poor. Whilst the two Boards are naggling over the question as Lo who should make the necessary inquiries, the children's education is being neglected The matter is one which might be settled in an hour, if a joint committee composed of deputations from the two Boards were to meet and con- sider how the preliminary inquiries should be made, and who should make them. Don't, pray, stand upon the order of the doing of iz, but get it done.

They have a way of their own in Buckley- street, Warrington, of inflicting punishment for certain offtnces, but the magistrates do ' not approve of the law being taken out of : their hands. Mary Weaver was bound over to keep the peace on Monday for having created a disturbance by burning Maggie Johnson. She had not burned Maggie liter- ally; she had set fire to some straw which was supposed to represent the erring sister. Maggie objected, and used such bad language in stating her objection that she too was brought before the magistrates, and was fined. On the whole, it must be said that the burn- ing process isn't satisfactory ; it didn't in the old days make witches any better, and it cannot be said to-day that it has improved ' Maggie Johnson. . i

WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—Up to the present the names of 300 persons have been enrolled as borrowers of wake from the library, and so far 500 books have seen issued. The interest in the reading room is still main- tained, there being 700 readers present on Saturday last. Bell, formerly curate of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, but now vicar of Was. dale, Cumberland, preached morning and evening to good congregations. Specially selected hymns were sung by the choir and scholars. VICE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday Richard Connell, a middle-aged man, who lived at Lugs. dale, was charged with having been on the premises of a labourer named McDonald, in Grenvilie-street, with intent to commit a felony. The circumstances of the case are unfit for publication. The prisoner was sentenced to three months' hard labour. WINES NATIONAL SCHOOLS.—The annual services were conducted on Sunday. In the morning the Rev F N Renal:lle, M.A., Vicar of Allerton, occupied the pulpit at nt. Paul's, and in the evening at ht. Mary's. The offertories amounted to about £l4. I SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—George Jones, of Princes street, who was a member of the Salvation Army, was fonnd dead in bed yesterday morning. His son was peace- fully sleeping beside him. About a week ago Jones caught a cold, bur it was thought he had fully recovered from it, and on Thursday everring he retired to rest about 11 o'clock, carrying with him a limp and a " IVar Cry," which it was his castom to read in bed. He was then apparently in good health.
