WATERED WHISKY AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty See- skins, on Thura lay, [Jenny Turner, of the Wellington Hotel, was charged with gelling whisky which was not of the sub- stance and quality demanded.—lnspector Wood proved the purchase of the spirit from Tuttle Gardner. the barmaid, and Superintendent Barker handed ins germ ificate from the county analyst, which stared that the whisky was 31 degrees under proof or adulterated to the extent of 6 per cent —Mr. Knoarlee, who defended, spoke of the defecclant'e respecta- bility, and the slightness of the adulteration.—The defen- dant having pleaded guilty, he was not permitted to explain the circumstances.—A fine of 20s and costs, 12s, was im- posed. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON AN INFANT AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Catherine Holland. a married woman, who resides in Grove-street, was charged with assaulting Michael Gamey. a child aged one year and five months. the son of John Carney, of Grove-street. It seemed there was some unpleasantnees between 'he defend- ant and the mother of the boy, and on Sunday morning the defendant called Mrs Carney "for everything." She finished her oheervations by throwing a stone, which Mrs Gamey avoided, hut the missile etruck :the child on the , head. The defendant admitted throwing the stone, but denied that it struck the infant. The Bench adjourned the coca for a fortnight, as .the child appeared to be seriously hurt. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES. On Monday, Thomas Smith, a rough-looking fellow, was brought before the Widnee magistrates, charged with having on Saturday night been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street. an-I with assaulting and resisting P.C. Cummings in the execution of his duty. It seemed that the prisoner was drunk and creat- ing a -disturbance in Merseysstreet by expressing a desire, in a very noisy fashion, to fight with several men who were present. As he would not desist. Cummings took him into custody, and he proceeded along very quietly until Parr's Bank, in Victoria-road was reached. Here one of his "mates" shouted "I would not let a bobby take me so easily," and the prisoner threw himself upon the ground and kicked the officer in a very violent fashion. He also bit his finger. After a prolonged struggle the prisoner was broneht to the police station. For being drunk a fine of 10$ and costs Wag irnpoeed, and for the assault the prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. NavrroN DivisioN.—At an extraordinary meet- ing of the Liberal "300" of the Newton Division held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Thurs- day evening week, a vote of entire confidence in Mr. Gladstone as leader of the Liberal party was unanimously passed, and the secretary was in- structed to forward the resolution to him at once. WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS.—The express saloon steamer, " Lancashire Witch," is advertised to make special daily callings from Liverpool to the Isle of Man and back at cheap fares. This new boat, built expressly for this service, is most replete in accom- modation for the convenience and comfort of pas- sengers. The times of sailing, fares, &c., will be found in our advertising columns. RAILWAY EXTRNSION AT WIGAN.—Sir Edward Watkin and some other directors of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company had an interview on Thursday at Wigan with a number of representative gentlemen who are asking the company to extend the Wigan Junction Railway through the town northwards. It was stated that great inconvenience and loss were being suffered by reason of the want of an alternative connection with Preston and the North. Sir E. Watkin said the powers his company possessed were granted by Parliament on the strength of evidence as to probable traffic, but their expec- tations had not been realised. The line already made cost double what was estimated, and it had paid little more than working expenses. It was at pre- sent practically boycotted by their great competi- tors, the London and North-Western and Lancashire and Yorkshire Companies, and it was not allowed to enjoy the traffic for which it was created. The directors would see whether a start could not be made with the extension, but they relied on those locally interested to remove the present boy- cotting. ACTION BY PENKETH FLATOWNERS. The only case of public interest tried at Widnes Court on Friday, before his Honour Judge Thomp- son, was one in which Messrs. Hill and Grundy, flatowners, of Penketh, sued Richard Abel, flatman, of Runcorn, for the sum of £5, being the amount of damage done to the small boat of the plaintiff's flat "Diana."—The defendant was-represented by Mr. J. Burton, solicitor, of Runcorn.—The facts of the case were as follows :—On the 20th of January the "Diana" and the defendant's flat, " Fanny," were at Eastham, having gone there for the pur- pose of loading sand. The "Diana," on grounding upon the bank, caused an eddy, into which the " Fanny " was dravion, smashing the small boat of the "Diana," with which it came in contact. The plaintiffs contended that Abel's boat was too near their boat, and that the captain (Wm. Gibbons) was not on deckots he ought to have been, or he could have prevented the accident.—Evidence was given for the defence showing that the captain was on deck at the time, and that the accident was caused owing to the "Diana" being too near the "Fanny."-.Mr. Burton contended that the defendant was not liable owing to the negligence on the part of the plain- tiffs men in getting too near the " Fanny," and also that as the accident had occurred at Eastham, within 430 yards of the shore, the Widnes County Court had no jurisdiction.— The Judge was of opinion that the centre of the river was the boundary of the two connties, and therefore the Widnes Court had no jurisdiction. With the con- sent of the plaintiffs he gave judgment for the de- fendant, without costs.

Loss OF A. LIVERPOOL SHIP AND ALLlTlewris.—The iron sailinc ship Comoro, of Liverpool. whibh left Newport on the 13th December for the Mauritius, has been lost with all bands. The vessel was built in Glasgow In 1804, and bad a net tonnage of 998 tons. Among those on board was Mr. Funk Pardon, a well•known South Wales I footballer.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Whitsuntide is near, so pack up your traps, you who have saved your sixpences; and, as Waugh says, "go to fresh places and see some fresh faces." Frisk it, my lads, in the fresh air by mountain, lake, or sea. Fun is worth more than physic.

The Dublin Corporation have declined to take part in the Jubilee Thanksgiving Ser- vice at Westminster Abbey. The people of Dublin are to be incluaed in the Jubilee Coercion Bill, and they do not feel thankful.

The Local Government Board is kind. Permission is given to Boards of Guardians to relax the "discipline and dietary of work- house inmates on the 2lst June." This may mean as to discipline a dinner, and as to diettry a champagne supper. Oh, its nice to be a pauper—once in fifty years. The brutal attacks which the Orangemen of Canada continue to make upon Mr. W. O'Brien are bringing discredit on the Domin- ion. Breaking the law by shameful assault on an unarmed visitor is a curious way of dis- playing loyalty! But Orangemen always were a curious set of people.

A carter named Rigby was drugged and robbed at St. Helens on Saturday ,evening. It is hardly necessary to say that he was in his cups when he was relieved of his money. "Oh. that men should put an eneiny in their mouths to steal away their brains l'"

The "Liverpool Echo" says :---" lodide of potassium relieves headache arising from cold in the head." This may be so, but, seeing that Io died of potassium, we rather tnink it would be better to give the drug a wide berth.

The 44 Echo" also tells of an Editor who searched for a lost pen, and. "bending down the top of his ear, discovered no less than fourteen penholders of various styles which he had llost during the past two years." Likely enough, but why does the " Echo " treat the public to these personal revela- tions ?

Chief Constables are at present in demand. Appointments have just been made at Burnley and at St. Helens; and there is one wanted at Blackpool. With such a prospect of rising in the ranks, who, for the future,i will dare to say, or sing, that "The policeman's lot is not a happy one."

Gambling amongst boys seems to be on the increase in Warrington. On Monday no less than sixteen boys were fined for breaking the law by playing at pitch-and-toss. This should be further looked to. Parents might do something as well as the police. Pitch-and- toss is not manslaughter, but it is on the same inclined plane.

Father Keller and Father Ryan, in Ireland, and the Rev. J. Bell Cox, in England, have beenceleased from gaol. It seems that in each case !there were informalities in connection with the imprisonment. "Some one had blundered." How would it be to lock a few of the !lawyers up? It would give them time to study the law; and meantime the rest of the I,communlity would breathe more freely.

"Going, going, gone'? " Such in brief will be the epitaph of the Beaconsfield Clcb, unless something or somebody saves it from the sale by Auction which is announced far next month. What think ye of this, ye Knights and Dames of the Primrose League? If you will not rush to the rescue, do, please, put on some sign of mourning; and sing, altogether, "Tis but a little faded flower."

It is seldom that a coroner's jury has to listen to such a touching story as that told by John Harrison, flatman, at an inquest held in Warrington on Monday afternoon. The great gale of Friday robbed him of his son, a lad of thirteen after both had endured great hardship on /the river. The boy literally died in his father's arms spent and broken by the storm. Henry Brolley, a man of thirty-four, also perished at the same time. The storm was one of the most terrible ever known on the Mersey.

PROSPERITY Or RUNCORN LODGE 10 G.T.—Brother E Davies, W.C.T., presided over the weekly meeting held in Regent-street Schoolroom, on Wednesday, and there was a good attendance. An enjoyable miscellaneous entertain- ment was given by the following: 'Brothers A Shingler, Hamersley,'E Davies, H Pilgrim, and Tlrox. WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS AT RUNCORN.—Although the jubilee celebration is so close upon us, en Whit Monday the children attending a number of the Snnday schools in the tows will parade the main thoroughfares as usual, accompanied by brass bands. Only tbe members of one friendly society will thus display themselves. The rail- way company intend to run excursions to various places t interest in the neighbourhood and on the Welsh coast. A Comormrar, .oansa.—At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Thompson, an application was made on behalf et the London and North-Western Railway Company, by Mr. ferrand, for the committal of Nathaniel Edwards, of the firm of Abbott and Co., billposters, Church street, in respect of a debt of £5 owing by the defendant, the balance of rent for coal office occupied by him in Tunnel-road, Edgehill. Liverpool. Mr. Werrand said the defendant lived ins house at •Rainforci, for which he paid VS a %year, and he travelled there to and fro by rail. Beyond that he knew nothing of hie means. He saw the defendant on Tuesday, but could not come to any arrangement; in fact he was abusive, and said the only way the cotarany could get any money was by taking their billpoeting from Beadle (his rival) and giving it to him. The Judge said he would in that case grant a commit- meat order. WIDNES GYMNASIVBI.—The annual general meeting of the members of the Widnes Gymnasium was held at the Alexandra Hotel, Widnes, on Friday evening. There was only a small attendance, amongst thost present beiug Messrs W E Vakden (who presided), T J Peters (treasurer) P t McMahon (secretary), 8 Beesley, T Fogg, R Johnson, J Wright, F Beattie, &c.—The Chairman having reviewed the progress of the gymnasium during the past season at some length, the treasurer read the report, whicta showed that the expenditure had exceeded the receipts by £7 Is.— A letter was read from Mr. Alexander, director of the Liver- pool Gymnasium, stating that he oonsidered the gymnasium had done very well for a first season.—A deputation was appointed to sea Mr. Holbrook Gragrell, sen., proprieter of the Baths A.ssembly Room, as to whether he could nut allow the use of tie room for the next season at a less rate. The appointment of officers was referred to a future meeting. FELONIES AT Ruscoaw.—At the Runcorn /Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Joist Brundrit, Henry Drew, alias Charles Rudd, was brought up on remand charged with having on the 15th February stolen a spirit level, the property of Robert Rathbone, contractor, of Northwich; a two-foot rule, three straps, and a pair of reins, the property of various worktnem—Rattibone and his brether, who are in partnership as builders and contractors, are at present en- gaged upon the erection of a tower at Norton for the Liver- pool Waterworks Company. The prisoner was employed there for several days. and after his departure the various articles were missed. The prisoner subsequently off-red the reins for sale to David Orolborne, a carter, and the other articles were found upon him when apprehended. As the primmer had been twice previously convicted he was com- mitted for trial to the Quarter Sessions.—Thomas Datton, an elderly min, was charged with having stolen a pair of trousers, a coat, and a watch, the prooerty of Mary Acker- ley, on different dates since the 14th February. When ap. prehended by Inspector Millington, pawn tickets referring to the watch and trousers were found in his ponession. The prisoner was remanded in order that his antecedents might he aacertained.

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT.EIINCORN.. stroet Willis, Bomb, .Elloomere-straet ; John Warm-
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT.EIINCORN.. stroet Willis, Bomb, .Elloomere-straet ; John Warm-

A fatal accident et a shocking description occurred at the works of the Rencorn Soap and.Alkati Company on Wed- nesday. The circunts acmes as revealed before Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, at the Greta*, Hotel, oo Thursday, were as follows : At the pr. seta Mr. 'Pawnee Kirkham, chemical engineer and contractor, 13 engaged in the erection of near buildings at the works. About a montn ego a dar- rick was constructed for the purpose of raising heavy weights, and it was moved about from time to time aft pC (melon requ'red. On Wednesday Thomas Ciarke, a lab turer, 38 years of age, whose house was in tauthertand-ntreet, had the control of the 01.rtick, and superlotenderi its removal . and fixture at a different spot. About eleven o'clock beam weighing about 15 cwt. was :dialed, asset Clarke, who was on the platform atoee, released hie lrod f the guy, in order to balance the timber which was heavirr at one ero than the other. The chaM cave a j-rk, and the timber lowered about a foot, and Chike, uot having a ti- bold of the b.-am, fell te the grouud, a distance ti 40 feet, alight- ing on his back. In his descent be came in cuntac, with a wooden cistern. He was at once conveyed to the house of I his sin .r. Mrs SArAil Cnmesree, et Sutneelaud-etreet, atnt Dr. Robinson and Dr. McDougall were quickly ia atten- dance. Death occurred at half past twelve.—Samuel Bux- ton, if 213, Bridgewater-it. foreman joiner to Mr. Kirkham, who bad been in the trade 36 or 37 years, deposed that the foot of the derrick stood on two pieces of wood, on a cross- piece six inches in thickness. There was a pia three inches long iii the foot of the derrick, but there was no socket la the cross-piece to receive the pie. After the accident he found that the derrick foot:had slipped, and was bedded in the ground. The blocks of wood were in position. It was' not usual to make a socket for the pin. He never knew one slip before. He accounted for the accident by the lurch of the chain, which was sometimes caused by the chain getting twisted in going through the blocks.—By Mr. Grice (the foreman): The deceased Axed the derrick to his own satis- faction, and if he had wanted anything to make it safer, the materials were all ready to his hand. He (witness) thought it Seas quite safe. Previous to the accident three or tour loads were taken up, two much heavier than the one that was then on the chain.—William Armstrong, of 33, Rutland.street, stated that he was on the top of the scaffold with the deceased, and he described bow, when the chain gave a jerk, Clarke had only held of the beam with the first joints of his fingers, and he could not therefore retain his grasp —The Coroner, in summing up, said he thought it would have been safe had the pin of the derrick been bedded in the wood upon which it was placed, hut the de- ceased Axed it himself, and that question did net arise.— Mr. Kirkham, who was present, said the derrick was safest in the manner in which it was constructed. Had the wood been soft enough for the pin to have bedded itself, the wood would save been splintered to matchwood.—The Coroner suggested that a, socket plated witb iron would answer the purpose.—Mr. Kirkham acknowledged this, but contended It would be no safer.-11 verdict of acedeotal death was returned.

; Ralph Gibson, Ashridge-street Bose Broughton, Warringon and Adam Taylor, Warrington. were now taken, and all dismissed on the same ground.—James Hoe- , rocks, ststioner, Irwell•lane, was charged with obstructing Bridge-street.—lnspecter Millington proved that the defend- ! ant had a stall on land almost opposite the office of W. Lightburn, on Monday, the 16th May, which was nOt a rnarket day.—Mr. Linaker took a similar objection that he bad taken in the former cases, and said, if necessarry, the • market inspector would prove that the ground had been oc- cupied by stalls for 12 years, and tolls receive.—The Bench dismissed this case also.—Superintendent Hollingworth gave notice that he should apply for a case to be stated for appeal.—Mr. Reynolds then said that in the case of Brit- land there was no doubt the law bad been broken. Did the superintendent press the case I—Saperintendent Honing- worth said he did not wish to press the case unduly. He would take their worships' decision.—Mr. Reynolds then dismissed Britland with a eaution that he must not loiter either opposite the "Glass Barrel," or any ether part of the town. lie mot keep moving on.

div.head: POLICE AND RUNCORN MARKET GROUND. IMPORTANT PROCEEDINGS. '
div.p: THE POLICE AND RUNCORN MARKET GROUND. IMPORTANT PROCEEDINGS. '

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, a number of stall holders on the ground opposite the Market Hall were sum- moned for obstructing Bridge-street, and as the matter was one of very great importance to the Board of Commis- sioners, great interest was taken in the cases. Mr. W. H. Linaker, law clerk to the Board of Commissionersoppeared for ten of the defendants, and 'asked that the case of Adam Taylor should be taken first. Superintendent Hollingworth objected. He regretted to say that the police had come in contact with the Commissioners, and be did not kaow what the ratepayers would receive in consequence.—Mr. Linaker remarked that if there was any soreness it rested with the police.—Mr. Reynolds (to the Superintendent) : Yours is the other view.—Superintendent Hollingworth : Yes.— Mr. Linaker said that in takine these proceedings the police had not had common courteey to communicate Witt] the Commissioners, who within the knowledge of the police had exercised the right of letting stalls on this ground from time immemorial. If the police bad any grievance at all they should have laid their complaint bekre the Commis- sioners, who were responsible for the care of the streets in the town, and who were as anxious as the superintendent of police could be that the traffic should not be impeded. He thought it would be a wise course for the Superintendent to withdraw the whole of the summonses, and to pat himself in communication with the Commissioners, and see what grievance there is. Don't let the police representing the county and the Commissioners representing the town be in conflict.—Superintendent Hollingworth said the police were not taking proceedings under the Towns Police Act, but were simply carrying out the Highway Act, which they had a perfect right to do for the safety of the public. He had I made it his busineae to communicate with the Market In- spector, showing him his,instructions, and he said he did not obstruct the highway. The matter was reported to the Chief Constable, and he (Superintendent Hollingworth) was acting directly under his instructions. The police hae no wish to become as annoyance to anyone, but for the safety of the public the chief constable directed these proceedinga to be taken.—Mr. Linaker said he regretted that the chief constable had not exercised the courtesy he usually did in carrying out his duties. If the chief constable had put eee.eif in communication with the Board the matter might have been fought out in a proper manner before the Court of Quarter Sessions. It was a question which affected the great right which the Commissioners claimed was vested in them of letting stalls in Bridge-et.—Mc. Reynolds : It seems a very large question. It is a pity that two pnblic bodies which are supposed to act for the public good could not agree together. Was there no way of settling the matter ? —Superintendent Hollingworth : No, sir, we have taken the opportunity of warning tha public and the Market Inspector that this is an offence committed under the Highway Act.— Mr. Linaker: The highways in Runcorn are under the di- rect control of the Runcorn Commissioners. He added that if the Superintendent wished to have the question settled in a proper manner he should have summoned the Market In- spector, and then the Commissioners could have taken steps to uphold their rights. The summonses were then pro- ceeded with. The first case was that of Henry Britland, a youth, who was charged with obstructing Bridge•street.—P.C. Milling- ton deposed that at a quarter to seven on the evening of the 14th May Britland was in charge of a potato engine and donkey, which were !tending on the right hand side of Bridge-street, opposite the "Glass Barrel." At seven 'o'clock he told the youth he had been there long enough, but he, nevertheless remained until a quarter past eight. The street was crowded with persons, and it was dangerous for people, or horses and traps to pass along. Inspector Mil- lington said be had previously cautioned the defendant. Bridge-street was a public highway, and was used as such every day in the week.—The defendant said he only ar- rived at the spot at seven o'clock, and after the constable had spoken to him he went home and told his mother, and when he returned, the constable ordered him away.—The mother corroborated the boy's statement. She said for six years they paid toll to stand where the boy was.—By Superintendent Hollingworth: She paid tell on thie oc- casion.—Mr. Reynolds : Did you think that what you paid gave you a right to stand at that side of the street ?—I don't know; Mr. Dutton has always collected toll of us.— At the reqmest of Superintendent Hollingworth, Inspector Millington was re-called to prove that the highway was used in preference to the market provided by tbe Commis- sioners. The Inspector said at the time this offence was comulitted there were not 20 peeple in the market, includ- ing the persons in charge of the stalls. The highway was very crowded. sod mach business was being done there.— By Mr. Reynolds: During the 17 months be bad been in Runcorn the market was in the same half empty state and the street very lively every Saturday night --John Cron- shaw, greengrocer, was charged with having, on the 14th May, unlawfully obstructed the free passage of Bridee- street. He pl aded not guilty. Mr. W. H. Linaker de- fended.—Sunerintenclant Hollingworth said be should sub- mit that market stalls and everything else which made the road less commodious and less convenient for the public was an obstruction, and that custom would not avail even if it extended over 50 years. The custom must be within legal memory, and that would reach further than the reign of Richard the First. Although be was not a lawyer, he co:,tended that the erection of these stalls on the highway could not be upheld.—lnspector Milltneton de- posed that on the 14th inst., between helf-past two and three o'clock, he saw the defendant at a stall erected on the left hand side of Bridge-street. opposite the market, and be occupied the footpath in attending to his business. The defendant said be bad paid toll, and the market inspector had placed him there. The stall was there until eleven o'clock at !tight. He considered that the stall was an ob. 1 struction, because people had to stand in the road te do business at the stall, thus causing great danger to horses and traps.—By Mr. Lineker: 'The road was formed of macadam. In front of the market there was a length that was done with setts. 7bis stall was on a piece of land Paved with sette.—Mr. Linaker said that prior to the build- ing of the market hall, the market was held in Bridges street from a little below Wilson's Hotel down to Mersey- street, and tolls were taken for stalls. In 1853 the Com- missioner?, to meet the growing requirements of the town, erected the market ball. But the marker hall was not suf- ficient, and never had been sufficient, for the stall holders who frequentre the market, and the Commissioners bad continued to exercise their right of placing stalls in convenient positions down Bridge-street as occasion required it. When the Commissioners tiought the market hall site, Bridge-street was much narrower than it was that day. It was narrower by the distance from the market ball to the outside of the setts previously mention d. He claimed that the Gimmissioners had a perfect right to let stalls on that land, and he argued that the Bench bad no jurisdiction.—Mr. Reyntdde said he quite remembered the street before the market was built —Mr. Linaker said it Wee not fair that the county should throw the responsibility of deciding a case like this upon the local bench.—Stmerin- tendent Hollingworth contended that no custom Mr. Linaker had cited would oust their worships' jurisdiction.—Mr. Reynolds remarked that the market was private Dr.. perty.—Superintendent Hollingworth: But the public having used the road .for over twelve months, it is dedicated to die use of toe public, and this rand, you will bear in mind, has always been used.—Mr. Linaker : It is a question of title—Alter some further conversation, the Bench dismissed the eatIIMOOS on the ground that the mag- istrates had no juriedlction.—Summonses against Ann White, Trinity-street ; Michael McGrath. Bridgewater.

Colscel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting of this Board held on Tuesday, when there were pre-sent the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs Mc- Intyre, P. Speakmin, S. Taylor, E. div.head: JUBILEE TREAT TO Th INMATES.
div.p: THE JUBILEE TREAT TO Th INMATES.

The Rev, J. Lockwood said he felt onfident that the mo- tion of which be had given notice b ould meet with the universal approval of the inecnOers. He was sure that not one of them would like to meet there on Jubilee day, the fiftieth anniversary of Her Majesty's coronation, especially as it was announced as a general holiday. Not only so, but it would be &Whitely disloyal on their part if they atten- ded such a me6ting on that day. It so happened that the 21st June was the day on which the Board should meet, and be had to prolapse that the meeting be deferred to Thursday, the 23rd June.—Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion.—Mr. Parr said he intended to have a holiday the whole week—(laughter)—and he moved that they disposed with the meeting altogether, and only have a meeting at the mouth's end.—Mr. Lockwood asked what about the

poor people. The relieseng officers would want their cheques arguing—Mr. Parr said they could be generous for once and sub.cribe the money amongst themselves. (Lauehter.)—The motion was carried unanimensly.—The Deputy Clerk read an order issued by the Local Govern- ment Board authorising the Quardians "to make each reasonable modidcation In the regulations in force in the house with regard to discipline, acid diet of the eroor people as might seem to the Board suitatile tor the occasion of the Jubilee." Tee Deputy Clerk remarked that they could give the inmates champagne according to that.—Mr, Lock-word: That wcald not be reasonable.-Mr. Fairhuret said theybito rer many holidays and jubilees that a working day or two more would be better.—Mr. Speakman inquired if they could not postpone the treat to the inmates until Thursday, the day of the meeting.—Mr. Hadfield: I think we shall have no time for feasting on that day. We shall have plenty of work to do.— the Deputy Clerk: We shall be getting sober. by that day.—Mr. Lockwood moved that in accordance with the general order of the Local Government Board, the inmates have something more than ordinary on "Jubilee Day," such as they had on Christmas Day, for instaece. Lady Broake had written to him aeking him whether anything would be done to give the young children 13.)1ne "Jubilee treat.'' She added,"! do'nt think that the rest of the inmates deserve one or ought to have any treat wbatever."—la reply to a question from Mr. Hadfield, Mr. Lockwood said he did nnt think Lady Brooke made her remarks dictatorielv. Ihe letter was quite private, bat he said he would bring it before the Board. If they decided to have the treat general, he should be able to write to Lady Brooke saying her letter was read in full and her views were set forth.—Mr. War- burton seconded Mr. Lockwood's motion to give a treat to the whole of the inmates.—lt was carried unani- mously.—A committee consisting of the Heys. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, and Messrs. Mclntyre, Speakman, Parr, Taylor, Wallington, and Aaron, was appointed to make the necessary arrangements.

div.head: A. VISIT TO PAIITASAI'II.
div.p: A. VISIT TO PAIITASAI'II.

The following report was read :—A deputation consisting of Messrs. P. Speakinan and E. A. Wallington was ap- pointed by the Board to visit, for the first time, the Catholic Orphanage, at Pantasapb, where, daring the last four years. several children from the Runcorn Union have from time to time been inmates, and now one named Margaret Corcoran, of Runcorn, aged 15 years, was about to leave for service. As Mr. Speakman was unable to go, the Rev. J. Lockwood went in his stead. The deputation was most courteoesly received by the Mother Superioress, and her Deputy. The girl was brought into the committee-room, when the deputation had a privste interview with her. She looked very healthy, strong, and cheerful, and gave most satisfactory answers to all the questions put to her. The Mother Seperioress afterwards informed the deputation that the girl was leaving for service on the following day to .t Mrs. Gardener, of No. 1. St. Ignatius-square, Presto'', Lancashire, and would be taken as far as Liverpool by a Sister of the College, and there received by a Sister from Preston, and delivered to her new home. The Orphanage has been founded 25 years, and contains children from all parts and union F—besides our own there being orphans from Chester, Prescot, and West Derby. The Orphanage is very extensive both as regards buildings and grounds, and every- thing both within and without is beautifully kept, and re- flects very great credit upon the management. All the children look well in every respect, and are thoroughly well cared for.—Mr. P. Speakman moved, and Mr. Aaron seconded, that the expenses of the deputation, amounting to Lila be paid.—Carried.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES QUESTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE SCHOOL FEES QUESTION AT RUNCORN.

The Deputy Clerk read the fellowing letter :—" Runcorn, School Board, Town Hall, Runcorn, May 11th, 1881 Sir,—l am directed by my Board to draw your attention to the fact that some three or four months ago your inquiry officer for this township discontinued to carry out the work of his office—having since then refused to entertain the applications of poor parents for payment of their chil- dren's school fees by the Guardians. I need not cite cases as tbe officer admits the facts and says ha is acting in ac- cordance with instructions. The consequence is that many children who had previously been attending school regu- larly, and who ought to be doing so now,are unable through the poverty of their parents to obtain admission, and their education is interrupted at a time when they ought to be preparing for the forthcoming examioationn. As it is pos- sible the orders given to your officer may have been issued under a mieapprebension, I am to ask that you will be so good as to bring the matter before your Board as early as convenient for reconsideration, and acquaint me with their decrsion. I am, sir, your obedient servant. Geo. Moss, clerk. Linaker, Esq., Clerk to Runcorn Board of Guardians. The Deputy Clerk explained that prior to the building of the Board Schools at Runcorn the relieving officer made inquiry into all cases where application was made for the payment of school fees. Since the building of that school where there was accommodation for both boys and girls and infants—if be was rightly informed certainly for boys and girls; the Guardians thought that as the School Board had DOW accemmedation of their own in which they could place children whose parents could not pay fees, after due in- quiry had been made by their officers. The Guardians ought nct to be troubled to make inquiry into such cases. , The School Board had their own inspectors..'.-Mr. Speak- man : Is it not the fact that they have not got a master ? The Deputy Clerk : They advertised for a master; then they dropped that idea all at once, and appointed only a ertiAress. They have a boys' school, but no master.—Mr. Taylor said he understeod the School Board had no power to pay fees,—The Clerk replied that the School Board had I their own officers, and these officers ought to make inquiry , about these cases. In Prescot the matter was managed by a small committee of the Gaardians and the School Board, and the School Board officer made the inquiries. It Ward had to make the inquiries they would have him applying for an increase*? salary. Two months ago Mr. Handley and Mr. Insisoo, and he believed the school attendanco officer, waited upon him at Frodsham, and he then told th-in that if thee would apply in a proper manner to the Guardians and offer some suggestion there was no doubt the Guardians would consider It. lie had heard nothing farther from them until that letter, and they now made no suggestion.—Mr. Aaron asked why the Guardiana should keep a man to do School Board work.—The Clerk reNarked that the payment of fees was immaterial to that Bea-d, as Guardians because the township of Runcorn would ii tve to pay the money. The Guardians had not get the machinery for carrying out the work and the School Board had.—The Chairman said they seemed to think in Runcorn that as the fees were paid through the relieving efficer be ought tr• I satisfy himself that they ought to be paid.—The Clerk : It 'is a mere accident that the school attendance officer and relieving officer are one and the same person. But suppose , Ward was not a school attendance officer he would still ; be called upon to pay these fees, but he would not be called , upon to make these inquirles.—The Chairman said Ward had to bring cases before the Board and te tell the Guar- diens why he asked for the relief.—The Clerk again stated that it was the dray of the officers of the Runcorn School Board to make inquiries. A small committee could be ap- pointed from the Guardians to confrr with thole officers and pre.ent the accounts each Board day.—The Deputy Clerk : The Runcorn township Guardians could be the committee.—Mr. Speakman suggested that a letter be sent in reply stating the clerk's contention.—Mr. Lockwood moved as the Runcorn School Board seemed to be at re standstill that the Runcorn Guardians be appointed a Com- mittee to deal with the question.—The Clerk suggested that it would be best to reply that a deputation from toe School Board were asked two months at° to submit a scheme, and that this had not been done. In the meantime they could ascertain exactly what scheme they had at Prescot.

- - _ W ARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. . .
.. ----.— - - MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmerel. Alder- man Harrison, and Councillors Greening and J. Pier-

point. POLICE Assauvr.—Edward Sauce, a labourer, was sent to prison for a month for drunkenness, and for having assaulted P.C. Caldwell, in Scotland-road, on Satnrday night. . DISTURBING TEE PEACE.—Winifred Cr e i Brldeq Kelly, two young women, were summoneci for creating a disturbinca. They were ejected from a public-house while under ths influence of drink, and commenced quarrelling to- gether. The magistrates ordered that each should find a surety for their good behaviour for the next six months, or in default suffer imprisonment for seven days. Mary Flannigan and Catherine Gray were each fined 5s and costs for a similar offence. MISCELLANEOUS.—The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—Daniel Christy, fined 10,4 and costs; Mary Lockett, fined Ws and costs; Samuel Thompson. fined 5s and coats; and Mary Enockton, ordered to pay costs.—John Fell, summoned for furiously driving, was dismissed with a caution.—For obstructing the footpath in Buttermarket- street, by allowing 24 cases of ale and porter to remain on it for upwards of an hour, John Liddle, licensed victualler, was fined 2s ad and costs. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton and Mr. E. J. Guest. _

THEFTS.—TWO girls named -Connor and Richardson were charged with having stolen a cashmere dress from a house in Mersey-street. Connor was sent to prison for seven days, and Richardson was dismissed with a caution.—Rich- ard Bosco (18), was charged with stealing from the office of Messrs. Rvlands Brothers, wire manufacturers, on the day previous, a jacket, value ss, the property of William Whit- taker. The coat was left in the office on Friday night, and was missed on the morning following. Prisoner pleaded guilty and was sent to prison for a month. DRCNBEINTNESS.—Mary Nicholson was sent to prison for seven days for having been drunk and disorderly in San- kev-street on the previous day. .WEDNE9IAY.—Before Councillors J. Pierpoint and R. W. Francomb.
BEGGlNG.—Willians Buck, for begging in Sankey-street, was sent to prison for seven days. FUIDIY.-14efore Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and _ _
Dr. G orna:11.

BEGOINCI.—Martin Kelly was charged with begging in Sankey-street on the evening previous. When apprehended he bad Bs Sd in his possession. Sent to prison for seven days—Thomas Deasey, charged with a similar offence, was dismissed on promising to leave the town. DRIINICENNESS.—EIiza Smith, who made her 24th ap- pearance, was sent to prison for a month for drunkenness.— For similar offences Mary Moran was fined 5s and coate, John Patten 51 and costs, and Edward Crosby 5s and costs. OBSTRUCTIONISTS.—Sarah Blease, a young woman, WAS summoned for wheeling a truck on the footpath in Frog- hall-lane, on the 14th inst. thus causing an obstruction to passengers. She was fined 6.1, including costs.—JAmes Leigh was similarly dealt with for wheeling a hand cart on the footway.--Hugh Ebenezer Hawthorn was summoned for causing an obstruction in Winwick-street by allowing an oran,w box and several tubs to be on the pavement. A fine of 53, including costs, was imposed. ALLEGED ASSATJLT.—John Mannion was summoned for assaulting Mary Jane Ellis on the 21st instant. Defen- dant alleged that complainant hit him first. Case dis- m is. ed. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Edward Fenton and Thomas Cooper were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Winmarleigh-street. They were ordered to pay 7s Ed each, the costs, be bound over in their own re- cognisances to be of good behaviour, and to each stand as surety for the other in the stun of £s.—James Wright was su.nmoned for disturbing the peace by fighting in Butter- market-street, on the 21st inst. He denied having commit- ted the offence. He was ordered to be bound over in his own recognisances, and pay costs. ELEEVING OVT.—William Harper, otherwise Titchett. was brought up on a charge of sleeping in a brick field, off Bewsev-road, without visible means of subsistence. It tran- spired that prisoner had received permission to sleep in the brick field, and he was therefore dismissed.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. C. Reynolds and G. L. Davies. _ _

OCCASIONAL LICENSE. —Henry Jackson, of Wilson's Hotel, was granted a license to sell intoxicating liquors at a public ball at the Public Hill on Whit Monday evening. WATWABDENS' LICENSES.—MI. H. G. Linaker Applied on behalf of his father, Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Daresbury Highway Board, for waywardens' licenses to cart in the district of that Board. A WOMEN'S Row —Martha Alice Jackson was summoned for assaulting Mary William, a married woman, of Penketh- lane, en the 11th inst. The case had been adjourned from this previous week to enable the couple to produce cot-. robotative evidence, and Mary Jane Brannon and Alice nothwell were called —The defendant alleged that the complainant threw her bedding into the street, struck her a blow on the bead that caused a wound that bled for several houts.—A fine of ss, and costs 16 %or seven days' imprison- ment, was imposed. The defendant went to gaol. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—WIN. Corker, Back Mersey-street, was tined 6d, and costs Si 6d, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-hones to be on fire. OnsrunertoN.—Wm. Hughes was convicted of obstruct- hog the footpath in High-street on Sunday evening the Bth fast, and on the evidence of P.C. Woolley he was fined ss. Damm.—James Kerley and a young man named Heyes were each fined 10s and costs for drunkenness.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS TIMRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gasket!, junior, and Mr. A. Fletcher. DiapNAENNEss.—The following persons were each fined 54 and costs for drunkenness :—Yatrick Irviue, James Dillon, Etlzabeth Broxton. ASS&Vl.T.—Bridget Weir, of Marsh-street, was convicted nf having assaulted Rose Mooney, of Nelson-street, on the 23rd inst., and she was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' hard labour.

TERRIBLE ATTEMPT TO MURDER A S'PrEETREA RT.—A most determined attempt to murder was committed in Leeds on Wednesday. James J. Perry, a respectably connected young man of a, out 24 years, whose home is at Cleckhea- ton. has for several weeks been employed as a printer at the works of Messrs. Butterworth and Hope, Leeds. -During that time he has kept. company with a girl a few years younger than himself, named Emily Jewett, who worked at the same establishment, and lived with her Parents at 37, Blenheim Place. About three weeks since Perry asked the young woman to marry him, and proposed the keeping of a publichouse. The girl objected, and a fortnight since she refused to have anything mere to du With him. After this Perry twice or thrice showed her a revolver, with which he threatened to shoot either her or himself if she did not assent to his proposals, but she still refused. On Wednesday afternoon the young Man made a final appeal to Miss Jowett, but she said she would have ne Shore to do with him. An hour later Parry deliberately walked IM to the girl and fired six bullets into her head and neck, one of them going through the temple and out through the forehead and the others remaining lodged in her ihead. She was removed home. OR Thursday, at Leeds, Perry was remanded for a week. The young woman remains in a precarious state, and her depositions have been taken.

WIDNES 2ND TEAM V. GAIISTON IST.—This match NM played at Widnes on Saturday in bitterly cold weather, and resulted in a limn for the home team. Winning the choice, Widnes sent in the visitors, who played one man short. Dixon and Gough were sent in fist on a fairly good wicket, when the former received a vorker from W. Kershaw which sent him back to the pavilion, 1 for G. Moss Jackson now joined Gough (when the latter was badly missed by Thorpe, who had the ball clean in his bands but could not hold it),. who, afterwards proved rather expensive. Both batsmen played accurate cricket, and notwithstanding constant change of bowlers carried the score to 55, before the separa- tion came, when J. liershaw caught Gough from Oakden. Shortly afterwards Jackson's wicket fell in a similar man- ner from the same bowler. The remainder of the wickets fell like ninepins, but not quite so quickly. W. Kershaw and Oakden both bowled well, the former taking 5 wickets for 16 runs and the latter 4 wickets for 14 runs. The in- nings closed for 71 runs. For Widnes W. Kershaw and Parkinson were the first to bat, and in a very short time Kershw came to grief from a good ball from Jackson. Thorpe now joined Parkinson, and a slight stand was made, when Thorpe's wicket also fell. Parkinson soon afterwards I followed suit for a useful 15. The next batsman did nothing of any consequence until Burgess came in, who appeared to be in his old form, and played fine steady cricket for his 25, runs, not out. Mahar also added a useful 12; not oat. For the visitors Moss Jackson did the meet execution with the ball, 6of the eight wickets falling to his credit. Ths match concluded in a win fer Widnes by 9 runs, with two wickets to fall. Score : Garte'row. NOTES BY THE WAY. The meeting of the representatives of Lancashire arid &ova at Manchester, on Monday, did not seem to excite much interest amongst the devotees of cricket, and the play was not of a very exciting character. The visitors were not by any means the strongest team their county can supply, and in batting capacity the were particularly weak, and went down rapidly before the bowling of Watson. All were out for the somewhat meagre total of 74. On the Lanca- shire side some creditable scores were registered, the captain, A. N. Hornby, running up 15, J. Eccles 38, Robin4en 27, and C. H. Haigh and Yates, neither of whom were out, 24 and 18 respectively. The Lancashire total was 146 with two planers to bat. Play was resumed on Tuesday, when the home team ran up their score to 154 In their second innings Sussex added an additional SI to their score, leaving Lancashire in need of only two points to win. These points were quickly added by Baker, and the game ended, Lanca- shire winning by ten wickets. The play in the match Leicestershire v. Cheshire was re- sumed on Saturday, but could not be brought to a conclusion owing to the boisterous weather. Leicestershire managed, however, to run up a total of 158, and Cheshire showed a respectable 59 for three wickets. St. Helens did not make a, creditable appearance at Aig- burth on Saturday, when they met to play Liverpool. The visitors arrived minus three good bats, and as might natn• rally be expect4d, the remainder of the team made a poor show. The eight wickets fall for a total of 32, F W Fidler being top scorer with 7 not out. The home team was a very strong one, including as it did the brothers H B and D Q Steel, Patterson, Remble, Richardson, drc. On going in to bat they ran up a score of 109—of which F William- son scored 42. Butler bowled well for St. Helens and took six wickets for 52 runs and A Sim took 4 font runs. If St. Helens had mustered m its full strength the probability is there would have been a great difference in the result of the match. The St. ILlens ".2nd team met Runcorn at Denton's Green, and the Runcorniane were crushingly de- feated. The visitors only notched 13 runs, the bowling of Edwards and Johnson for the home team being excellent, the former taking four wickets for four runs, and the latter four for nine. The home team scored 77. Liverpool Press and Sutton played a drawn game at Sutton, the Press scor- ing 72, and Sutton 42 for three wickets. A meeting of the Executive Committee of the West Lan- cashire Rugby Union was held at Liverpool on Monday evening. The chair was filled by Mr. W. S. France, of Wigan, and delegetes from the following clubs were present: —Warrington, Litherland, Southport Olympic, Wigan, St. Helens Recreation, Widnes, Walton, and IL Wilcock, bon. treasurer, and F T. Parry, boo. secretary. A letter was read from Mr. G. R. Hill thanking the union for the kind courtesy shown him during his visit to Widnes. It was de- cided to distribute the following sums to charitable institu- tions, as under :—Wigan Infirmary, £l5 ; Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, £10; Stanley Hospital, Liverpool, £lO ; War- rington Infirmary, £lO ; Southport Infirmary, £lO ; Free Providence Hospital, St. Helene, £7 10s; St. Helens Cot- tage Hospital, II 10s; and £23 to be deposited in the bank to form a charity fund. It would almost seem that path racing is not going to ha popular this season amongst cyclists, the entries for the Whitsuntide events being as a rule extremely meagre. The match, Liverpool v. Gentlemen of Cheshire, was played on Wednesday. at Chelford, and a game resulted in an even draw, Liverpool scoring 206 against Cheshire's 117 for five wickets. Amongst the Cheshire players S. M. TUE PERILS OF THE MERSEY. VICTIMS OF THE BECENTETORM. Much is said and written about the-dangers of the' sea, and every now and then the world is thrilled with narratives of maritime disasters which stir strong sympathy, while such dangers as are faced. by those who navigate the tidal river that runs through Warrington are sometimes apt to be over- looked. But the perils of the Mersey exist just as, surely as do those of the open sea, and, nearly every gale that sweeps the country leaves a record of loss of either life or property, and sometimes both, sus- tained on this famous waterway. The gale of last, week was an instance in point, and the crew of the fiat -"Hero," which was out on the Mersey dur- ing the storm, experienced sufferings as terrible as, any mariner shipwrecked at sea. The " Hero " is a flat belonging to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, of St. Helens, is captained by John Harrison, of 4, Wakefield-street, Warrington,and on Thursday morning in last week she sailed from- Widnes to Eastham with a crew consisting• of the captain and two brothers named Brolley;.whose home is in Widnes. There was also on board &son of the captain's, bearing the same name, and who was but thirteen year, of age. Thus the boat' car-, ried four persons, two of whom were fated' not to- return alive. They were caught ,in the gale that sprung up on the Thursday night; and' continued, with such violence during the following morning, and the unfortunate navigators went through a period of terrible suffering. Driven to cling- for dear life to a portion of the ves- sel, two of them succumbed to starvation, one being the lad, who died in the arms of his desparing father, and the other being Henry Brolley. The two survivors would probably have met the same fate had not a schooner, that was also, in distress, rendered what assistance it could, and, as it proved, saved their lives. The dead body. of Harrison was washed from his father's grasp, but was recovered some hours later' and was brought to ie h home at Warrington, while that of Brolley was taken on shore in Hooton township. The County Coroner, Mr. Samuel Brighouse, was communicated with, and, Warrington being in, his district, he attended at the Bowling Green Ihn,. Bank Quay, on Monday, to hold an inquiry concern- ing the death of young llarrison. The only witness called was the father, who was painfully agitated,, and with the sympathetic object of sparing his feel- ings, the coroner took his evidence as briefly as was possible. During the recital given by the witness,. it was noticed that several of the jurymen were visibly affected, and the narrator was at times' scarcely able to control his grief. From the infor-- mation he gave to the coroner, and from what was; gathered at a subsequent interview that our repre- sentative. had with the bereaved man, we are. enabled to give full particulars of the disaster. At ten o'clock on the morning of Thursday, the 19th, instant, the Hero sailed from Widnes for Eastbann for a cargo of sand. That day the boat stopped at a. spot known as the "Suez,' near Spoke, and at night the wind veered round to the west, and commenced to blow a gale. Harrison, seeing, as he remarked, that it was going to be a rough shop, got his vessel, under weigh and navigated her to westward, under "Poo" Hall, for safety. At one o'clock on Fridb,y morning the vessel was put on the bank for loading purposes, and loading was commenced soon after two o'clock. A hailstorm then came on, and the , captain expressed the fear that the wind would change and blow from the north. They, however, continued work, and got a little over five tons of sand on board, when the captain told, the men to "knock off." as there was sufficient to lie atriinchor ' with. They then put their tools on deck, straightened the flat, and made her as safe as possible: On ac- count of the driving of the wind it was floodtidh at six o'clock, an hour earlier than was expected, and the flat was thoroughly afloat, but should, the nar- rator said, have been "adry." Half an hour later the vessel swung to her anchor, and'Harrison, addressing his crew, said "Well, men we have-a sad case before us this morning; leave the anchor and the chain alone, and let her abide for half an hour. Leave her alone at her anchor, and' pay out chain." John Brolley thereupon remarked" We shall never get our anchor if we do," and Harrison. replied, ;Never mind, if we don't, we can -slip the chain and get in shore." They were then riding with fifteen fathoms of chain. In ten minutes the. boat began to take the anchor, and more chain was paid out, , but she grounded immediately afterwards at a Point ' that divides the Ellesmere Port deep. and the East- ward deep. Here the distressed vessel held for nearly half an hour, but when she 'bated from that position the captain resolved on amattempttobeach her on the west side of "Poo" hail, in, order that life and property might be saved. The windwas at that time blowing a gale from the northe and the captain put the fiat with her head to the north, facing the tide and wind. Unfortunately she flew round with her head to the-west, and consequently lay athwart the tide, while the small boat that she had in tow "lapped" round the stern and came alongside the flat. The sea, sweeping over the flat from the other side, dropped into the boat, which was immediately swamped. Had not the boat been brought exactly broadside with the vessel, it would have escaped. The boat being swamped, the men were confined to the flat, and the main chance of escape was cut oft. The fiat was now in a "ter- rible tempest," and Harrison's first thought was to strap his lad to his back and try to swim ashbre, but a kind of whirlpool that intervened rendered it impossible for the,thing to be done, for both man, and boy would be drawn in. The child never ram.- mured, and the. crew, the father with the lad clasped in his arms, took refuge on the "gaff' where they remained for over two hour& " God help me," exclaimed Harrison when giving his evidence, "the child died in my arms from starvation; he was not drowned.* Henry Brolley also died from starvation, sometime before the lad succumbed. Harrison had held the body of his son in his arms for about ten minutes after he- died, when a strong sea washed them both from the "gaff." He then clung to the mainstay,, but was through failing strength unable to keep hold of the body, which was washed from his grasp, The poor fellow continued the battle for life for anotherlialf hour, when a schooner came to the rescue and got him and John Brolley out of their difficulties. Brolley was nearly dead from exhaustion, and was not brought round to consciousness for ever four hours after he was rescued, The captain of the rescuing schooner, which was itself in distress, and his crew, treated the exhausted men with every kindness. Harrison, who could not rest until he had found the body of his boy, recovered it sometime afterwards, and ultimately brought it home with him to War- rington. In answer :0 questions, Harrison, who appears to be an earnest, God-fearing man, informed our representative that he had been a waterman all his life, having been, apprenticed to that vlication at the age of eleven years. The "Hero '' always

JUBILEE MATCH.—FLEMINOS' V. REYNOLDS' EMPLOYES. —The annual match between the two works took place on Saturday last in beautiful weather, but there were not many spectators present on account of there being so reacts foot- ball of late. Both sides had whipped together a strong team, Reynolds' losing stronger in the first division than their opponents. Right' and Adamson were the resp•ictive captains, both being old Warrington players. In the first half Rigby played with the son in his favour and went off with a good dash, and for a short time the Reynolds' tine was in danger. Ultimately Daniels removed And Ruby missed picking up, this being followed by a lot more misses on the parts of Reynolds', which resulted In Gilligan being within an ace of scoring. The all white, however, relieved their lines and took play to centre, Wilcox patting in some good work. Rigby next received a pass, but was tackled by Daniels before making mach headway. Some fast play en the part of Fleminge' next took play to line, and Adamson failing to bold let them in for a try, Rigby failing at an easy place for goal. Up to half time play was very evenly contested, no other point being scared. Crossing over Reynolds' evidently meant to equalise matters, for they played with great determination, and their supe- rior strength at length began to tell on their lighter opponents, as for a long time they penned them in their 25. Rigby and Wilcox relieved, and White put in a good kick to centre. From here Rigby made a dashing run, sad in- vaded Reynolds' quarters, but Donohue and Lightfoot put in a good dribble past centre. tiers some hot scrimmages were contested, and Donohue again broke away, the belt go- ing over the line. A well-contewed game ended in a draw, the score being Flemings 1 try, Reynolds 1 try and 1 minor. For Fleming, Rigby, Wilcox, and Potter were always Iwo- minent, and the same may be applied to Daniels, Donohue, and Bancroft on Reynolds' side. After the match both teams sat down to an excellent tea provided by Mr. and Mrs.- Massey, of the Roebuck Hotel. Mr. Gilbert and Mr. S.Wrigha; officiated as umpires, and Mr. Warren was the referee. Silence having been restored, Sir A. B. Ws.nirasn said: Gentlemen,—l thank you very much for responding to my invitation by be- ing here to-day. We shall proceed in a few minutes to Gateacre Green to unveil the bust of her most Gracious Majesty the Queen; but perhaps I may be permitted to detain'yon here for a short time upon another subject. Some years ago I purchased the site and buildings of these premises, which were formerly known as the Old Gateacre School, and it occurred to me thatthey might be made of practical utility as a library and reading-room. (Cheers.) On, mentioning the 'project to friends and neigh- bours the suggestion was received with favour. Hence the establishment of the Gateacre Institute —(cheers) an institution on a strictly non- sectarian basis—(loud cheers)—with the sole object of promoting:the social 'and intellectual welfare of the inhabitants of Gateacre and the neighbourhood. (Cheers.) A sufficient' period: has now elapsed to fully demonstrate the fact that this institution is appreciated by the inhabitants of the district, and capable of being carried on so, as to give general satisfaction, and I therefore determined, as part of this general Jubilee celebration, to complete its con- stitution by transferring the land, buildings, and property of the institutiom (comprising also the portion tenanted by the Little Woolton Local Board) to trustees, for the purpose of the institu- tion. (Loud cheers.) And Ttake this opportunity of returning my sincere thanks to the Rev. Canon Warr. Mr. Arthur B. Forwood, M.P., Mr. Harold Cunningham, and Mr. G. H. Robertson, who, in conjunction with my son, Mr..W. 11. Walker, and myself, have consented to act, as the first trustees. (Applause.) I now deliver •to the trustees the muniments and title of the premises, and I feel con- fident that under the able andi kindly supervision of the trustees, the Gateacre Institute will long continue of great and increasing utility to the in- habitants of Gateacre and the' neighbourhood. (Loud and prolonged cheering,) Mr. 11. CUNNINGHAM,' in , the' absence of Canon Warr, who was unable to be present through indis- position, received the institution on behalf of the trustees. Mr. GEORGB HuerasT, on behalf of the members of the institute, thanked Sir Andrew for this further token of his interest in their welfare. The ceremony over, Sir A.°, B. On either side of the bust of her Majesty a raised plat- form was erected, and these were also crowded with onlookers. Sir A. B. Wenxisn, who was Instily cheered, said : Ladies and Gentlemen,—We-are met here to-day to inaugurate the bust of her sMest Gracious Majesty the Queen, as a local and personal csntribution to the Jubilee celebration. (Cheers.) Her Majesty's happy and peaceful reign of half a century has wit- nessed an unprecedentgl advance in science and in I art, in literature and in , material prosperity.l (Cheers.) This advance has. -not been confined to a I portion of the people, but haspenneated all classesl of the community, and 'is atrikingly evidenced by the spread of education, amongst the masses, I and the extension to . them of political power. Much of this beneficial result has prob- ably been produced by, legislation and the machinery of publie institutions ; but a very important factor; and) one at first glance, perhaps, sometimes under-estimated, is owing to the personal and social infthence of her Majesty (loud cheers) assisted for so many years by the late Prince Co'nsort, and in later years by the Prince of Wales and other members of the Royal Family. (Cheers.) During the reign of fifty years, her Majesty, has devoted herself 1 to the social and individual welfare of her subjects, I and particularly of the poor,, the unfortunate, the sorrowing, and the afflibted, nothwithstanding the many calls upon her attention and generosity. (Cheers:), There is .hardly.' an institution in the country established for the alleviation of human suffering, or for the diminution of crime and im- providence, or the social and intellectual advance- ment of the masses which has not received mate- rial countenance, support; and attention from her Majesty:or her family.. This no doubt has contri- buted to largely secure the love and resi,ect of her subjeets. But there .has :been sonasthing more— namelys there has teen no .calamity, no disaster, no sorrow. to the very humblest of her subjects to warcle,which her Majesty has not extended a warm and loving sympathylhat has earned RA- her the true and lasting love of every section of the com- munity, and helped perhaps more thaw any other agency to bridge over the gulf separating class fromeclass—(loudmheers)—and, therefore, it ap- peare-to me that whilst Ivo should not omit to take parts in the national celebration which, has for its objet a scheme of Imperial magnitude. and impor- tance, we are also justified in expressing an indivi- dual thankfulness and rejoicing by ether means of a Ideal and persenal character. Cheers.) With this object in ssiew. I, have affordosl myself tho gratification of obtaining from the studio of Count , Gleichen this bust of' her Majesty insbronze, which,, with the village greem on which it, stands, I now , present to the Little Wbolton Local,'Board, in trust (Or the inhabitants ofr the district. (Loud cheers.) , Sir Andrew then, unveiled the bust amid gnat cheering. The bust is in bronzes and 3ft Glusin height. rids. artistically executed; and is a faithful likeness, of her Majesty. It stands on a handsome red granite Pedestal 7ft high, on which a vast-amount of labour has been expended. The pedestal is mounted with ! bronze. Oa the front there is as crown, and below' it the yean f`-1887-'''in bronze,, while on the other) side is tha,. following inscription:—" This monu- ment and village- green were, presented as a me- morial of the Jubilee of Vieioiiri, Queen of Great Britain anddreland and Empress of India, by Sir Andrew Barclay' Walken.Bart.,High.Sherift of Lan- cashire, 1886-7' Mr. IL Jump formally reeeived.the bust. div.p: NEW BOOKS. ea,

Messrs. Cassell & Co., have commenced to publish a new issue of Archdeacon Farrar's illustrated edi- tion of the "The Life of Christ," in monthly parts of sixpence reach. This marvellous work has now passed through no lees than thirty editions, and it is not too much to say that, with the constant inorease of teas dere of all classes, and especially of Sunday scholars' and teachers, it is destined to pass through as many more editions. No one could be better fitted for the great task of writing a Life of Christ than Archdea- con Farrar, and it is generally acknowledged that ha has accomplished it in a way which has exceeded the highest expectations. It is a learned record; and at the same time it is a popular one. The simplest rea- der finds himself charmed with a style which is glow • iug and picturesque, and he is led on and on with ever increasing interest; while the student has douhts resolved, difficulties removed, and crooked things made straight in a war which cannot but ex- cite admiration for the vast learning and research of the scholarly author. There is necessarily something in a work of this class which is more or less of a con- troversial kind; but if all controversialists will try to fellow the example of the Archdeacon and anon of Westminster. there will be less of bigotry and more of genuine Christian feeling in the world. Like Tennyson's hero, he wears his learning lightly as a fibwer, and shows himself throughout humble and reverent in spirit. Writing with the complete volume before us, we are bound to say that it is in every way a credit to Messrs. Cassell & Co. There are over I 3..00 illustrations of an authentic kind—many of' them being from photographs- taken in the Holy Land, and the result is that the volume may be said in this particular to stand unrivalled. The " Blue- trated London News," which is no mean judge in a matter of this kind says: "The book is rendered-let more useful, as well as extremely beautiful and, at- tractive, by the magnificent series of pictorial inns. trations with which it is now supplied in the present edition. Messrs. Cassell & Co. have spared no coat er care in preparing this noble volume. The views of places in Judea and Galilee, and ruins of buildings, of the towns and cities, Jerusalem. Bethlehem, Nam- reth, Tiberias, the supposed sites of Bethsaida and Capernaurn, and many localities of hallowed associa- tions, contribute the larger part of the illustrations ; beeidee many others which exemplify the customs, dress, manners, and habits of the people in that country. Maps, plans, and diagrams assist the topo- graphical explanations, and there are many small drawings of furniture, implements, and utensils- of daily life, which help the reader to a correct know- ledge of things mentioned in the Gospel narrative, or in the discourses and conversations reported- of Christ." It should be stated that there is issued in the first part a fine portrait. engraved in steel, of the Archdeacon Farrar. As showing the feeling with which the author entered upon the undertaking, we quote the following extract from the preface: -"After" he says, "I had in some small degree prepared my. , self for the task, I seized, in the year 1870, the earli- est possible opportunity to visit Palestine, and es- pecially those parts of it whioh will be for ever iden- tified with the work of Christ on earth. Amid thoee scenes wherein he moved—in the— - _ _

Holy fields,. Over whose acres walked those blessed feet, Which, eighteen hundred years age, were nailed For our advantaee, on the bitter cross— inthe midst of those immemorial customs wbieh re- call at every turn the manner of life He liired,—at ,Teratealem, on the Mount of Olives at Bethlehem, by j'acob's Well, in the valley of Nazareth, along the briatht strand of the Sea of Galilee, and on the comets of Pyre and Sidon—many things came home tome, for the first time, with a reality and vividness un- known before. I returned more than ever conErmed in the wish to tell the full story of the Gospels in such a manner and with such illustrationsas--with the aid of all that was within my reach of that knowledge which has been adeusnalating for ceuturies—might tend to enable at least the simple and the unlearned to under- stand and enter into the human surroundings of the life of the Son of God." How Archdeacon Farrar succeeded in his task is beet attested by the-constantly increasing demand for this Lae of Christ. We cor- &alb, commend the new issue to our readers-4: it is, astute been truly said, a book which has " come to be regarded as indispensible, not only to every Christian ' minister, Bible teacher, Sunday Seabee' teacher, or bead of family, but to every reader and student of the sacred text." "The Booke of Olde Manchester and Salford" is an unique production just pulilished by Mr. John Hey- wood, of Manchester. It is issued as a pictorial and literary guide to the sightseer at the Manchester Ex- hibition, and as mole it may be pronounced perfect in its way. But few who gaze at the representation of "Olde Manchester and Salford" at the Bahibition who will not feel that they would like to possess some permanent memorial, and the boole is exactly suited to this desire. The hietorical and, descriptive text is by Mr. 21.4 Derbyshire. TALB.A.,,,,and there is also an introduction by Mr. George Milner, President of the Manchester Literary Club. They " booke " abounds—indeed, it may be said to overflow with illustrations by .1. Langhare, W, Palmer, W. A. Fenn, and A. Darbyshire. AU of them are cleverly executed, and sane of them are very quaint and humourous. Author, artiste, and publisher are to be congratulated, on a publication which will increase in value when the Exhibition has ceased to be. "Poems selected from Heinrich Heino,. by Kate F. greekertt appears as the current issue of the Canter- bury Poets., It is an exceptional literary treat to be able to obtain these beautiful poems, in this chea? form. Andoire anticipate that there. will be quite a. run on the present editiou., The poems are prepared with a tea4thy and carefully prepared memoir which is in-itself worth the shilling, which is char, for the voinme. In the Oarnelot Series, also pu'etished by Mr. Wailer- Scott weltave the" Meditations .of Marcus Aurelitas,, translated+ from the Greek by derem7 Collier, revised with an, introduction and notes. by Alice Zioamern.l There are few persons who decerve. to be had in•re-, mounicTance so well as, the Empercr Aurelius, for. he left a legacy of inexhaustible riches in his " Medita- tions." He has been well described as " the noblest of Pagan Emperors," and puts modern princes to the blush alike by his precept and example.. The calm philosophical spirit which, these writinge reveal stands almost as meth in need el cultiyatica, to as when the "meditations "were written. The book will, delight those who would' breathe free air, and ele- vate their vision.

"The Life of Samuel Jblarkson 133,..Lieut.-Colowel F. Grant," reaches us in the "Great Writers" caries. There cannot, of course, be any life of Johnson—equal intenst to that written by his friend Losweil ; bat it ienot every reader in these swift.footed days who can find time to read Doe-well's life, to aay, nothing of ens7ecting the Inaceuraeiee which recent research has dieclosed. The .?resent volume is therefore opportune ; it erovrds the main facts of Dr. Johnson's life into some POO pagee,and is, altogether a very untertaining book. _ _

The Emigrant's Handbook to the British Colonies has been compiled by Mr. Waldemar Bannow as a labour of love, an& like most work executed under- such circumstances, it is well done.. For a shilling, the inteneting emigrant may obtain a trustworthy summary of just such information as he requires to know wi'h regard to Canada, New Zealand, Queens- land, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australi,a, Western Aualralia„ Cape Colony, and Natal. The Hand-book is published by Mr. Walter Scott, London. Messrs., Charles Sc Co., London, have issued three highly finished steel portraits of the Queen, The - ; first represents childhood, the second maidenhood, and I the third womanhood. Her Majesty at the age of eight and eighteen is charming; but we cannot say we are pleased with the portrait of her appearance some twenty years later. The portraits are very suitable for framing, and will doubtless be itt demand during the present year. "Dreams and Omens of the Derby" is a curious collection by Fortunatus, with "tips and omens for other places." it is in a double sense racy reading, and will be especially interesting to the sporting fraternity. The Scotch Free Church Assembly resolved on Wednes- day by 422 totes to 73 to again petition Parliament in fa- vour of the disestablishment and disendowment of the Es- tablished Church of Scotland.

Several excithg incidents in connection with the tithe agitation took place on Wednesday at Llangwm and Llan- rhaiadr, North Wales. The opposition was so strong that the sales had to beitbandoned. The Northumberland miners' strike was settled on Tues. day afternoon, at a conference of owners and miners, the man submitting to a reduction of 121 per cent and 61 per cent rePpectively• on different classes of coal. DErrrarmirE FlRE.—Early on Tuesday morning a fire broke out in a block of buildings in Tyrell-street, Bradford, jointly occfipiod by certain tradesmen and the Grosvenor Club. Nlano thousands of pounds worth of damage was caused by tl,e fire. FRIGHTFuL ExPLOsiON.—According to a telegram re- ceived at the Colonial Office from the Governor-General of Calnda, 36 Englishmen, 0 Scotchmen, 9 Welshmen, and, 5 Irishmen were killed in the rectnt, colliery explosion, at Nanairm, Vancouver Island.
