"Although unseen, my influence is felt,"rercarked the Evely flea. The mathematician's favourite season is the sum-mer. 'The milkman's'is the spring. ; Good resolutions, like a squalling baby at church, should always be carried out. "What's in a name ?" a recent traveller was heard to (111tclaim. ." Why, about the hottest country on the globe is Chili I" '

IWhat does a chiropodist mean when he advertises that he has "removed 'corns from several of the crowned heads of Europe?' A SIMPLE Sournott.—We are told that all the fifty millions of people of America could be put into the State of Texas without crowding. This is because they have a habit in Texas of suspending persons froirarees and telegraph poles. This makes more room below. A Wenn WELCOME.—A local divine relates with much gusto the unwonted honours paid him at a recently- attended funeral service. _ On his arrival the widower—.
chief mourner—arom and addressed the assembly as --•-- • • • . .

follows: "My friends, I have the pleasure of introducing to to ou the Rev. Dr. —. We'd better sing something. Suppose we try the Doxology." UST As EFFECTIVE.-4. paralytic young woman, who had been unable to walk for years, was conveyed to a revival meeting one night recently, and during prayer she suddenly arose, gave an ear-piercing shout, climbed over three pews, gained the aisle, and made a 'dash for the pulpit. It was not another faith cure, asoany per- sons in the congregation supposed. She had simply seen a mouse in a pew near her feet. _ _ ,_.

MADE IT WARN FOR Tau.—An Albuquerque (New Mexico) editor, who expected e; gang of lynchers to come for him about the middle of the night, i took him- self to the cellar, leaving a pet grizzly bear n his place In bed. The lynchers did not bring any light, but made a plucky attempt to get the bear out and lynch it, but gave it up after three of them had lost an eye apiece, two of them had suffered the loss of thumbs chewed off, and the other six were more or less deprived of skin. The man now has a great reputation of being a fighter, and the bear did not mind the work one bit.

A PLUCKY BEITISHER.—An English sportsman while partridge shooting, had his left band badly shattered through the bursting of his gun. On arrival the doctor exclaimed: "Well, you have made a mess of it. I must amputate it!" The patient readily submitted to the operation without chloroform, and on the doctor leaving the room with the severed hand, he was astonished at the unfortunate calling after him : "Doctor, I forgot to , say how proud I always was of that little finger, so please save it for me for a tobacco stopper!" Textrio THE HINT.—A resident of one of the French provinces had gone to pass a few days with some rela- tives in Paris. Becoming infatuated with t,he gay capital, he remained until patience on the part of his hosts ceased to be a virtue. Too polite to openly re-1 monstrate, they threw out a hint: "Don't you think, dear fellow," they said to the bore,." that your wife and children must miss you ?" "No doubt. Thanks for the suggestion; I'll send for them." NOT STOLEN.—A gentleman on his way home last Monday night at 9 o'clock met a negro boy coming- out of an alley with a chicken under his arm. He took hold of the boy, examined the chicken and, finding it a nice fat pullet, asked the boy if he had not stolen it. The boy replied: "No, sir; if I'd er stolen dat chicken I'd er had 'im in er bag, boss." The gentleman let him go on his way. BEAUTY UNADORNED.—"Woman is the most perfect work of nature," he said, as they stood looking at the moon through the parlour window. "Do you think so," she asked with a charming smile. "I do. The ma. jority of men think so. But women do not appear to have any idea of their own charms of person." 'What leads you to think so?" "Because they disfigure their beautiful forms with enormous bustles and put on their shapely heads shapeless structures of felt and feathers. Those who say women are 'vain are mistaken. They are not vain or they would dress simply and thus show off their natural charms to the best advantage." "I guess you never saw a fashionable young lady in her bathing suit, John." John said no more. The appearance • in literature of General John C. Fremont, the great "Pathfinder," has brought out an incident with reference to Mrs. Jessie Benton Fremont and a characteristic interview which she had with Pre- sident Lincoln. It occurred early in the war, when Fremont had command of something like ninety thou- sand men in Missouri, and an effort was being made to place General Prank Blair in command of half of them. • Mrs. Fremont hurried to Washington, to prevent this division of her husband's command. She called upon the President, with whom she had an exciting inter- view. It was not satisfactory to her, and, raising her hands in a dramatically threatening manner, she said, " Beware, Mr. Lincoln; we make Presidents !" Mr. Lin- coln was writing at his desk, and, as ,he listened to her declamation, without stopping the motion of his pen or moving a muscle of his face, he replied, with that grim wit for which he was so famous, "Pretty poor things, 'I guess!" DIDN'T KNOW BAKER—Yesterday forenoon as two men who had lived neighbours to each others on High-street for a year and walked down town together a hundred times met on Griswold-street one of them remarked : " Say, Green, drop into the bank with me for a minute. I want to be identified." "Certainly, certainly," replied Green, and they entered the bank and walked to the teller's window. "You identify this man as 'Baker, do you aSked the teller. "Baker ? Baker-? Yes, I believe that is his name? "Do you know it to be?" "No—o, but I've heard it was. He lives next door to me." "110 w much of a family has he?" got a family anyhow, and I see some children around:" • What does he do?" " Let's see. He's got an office of some sort down hare, but I can't say wthatle does." "Will you positively identify him as Baker ?" " Why—well—no, I guess not, I think he is, but he may be Barker, or Barkem, or he may not be the one I think I know. Excuse me, Mr. Baker; I'd be glad to oblige, you know, but I don't•know you, you know." Wog:murex SPOIL THE DINNEIL—An old war veteran, who had been through half-a-dozen campaigns, and was not very particular about what he ate, was invited out to a swell dinner party. t Ile sat almost directly opposite the hostess, and was painfully conscious that every move he made could be observed by her. Suddenly, at the height of the festivities, the veteran came across a caterpillar-in his salad. A furtive glance at't he hostess disclosed the fact that she, too, had .discovered the em- barrassing, Circumstance. It was a criticalmoment, but the old soldier was equal to the occasion. Without changinvt muscle he gathered up the caterpillar with a forkful,of thesalad and swallowed bcrthl The look of gratitude which he received from his hostess, a few I minutes later, warmed the very cockles of his heart. In due time the story leaked out, and when somebody asked the old campaigner how he liked caterpillar salad, the reply came like a hot-shot: "Do you take me for a man who would spoil a dinner party for a 'little thing like a caterpillar?"

Xettero to the Itttor. A QUETIONABLE APPOINTMENT AT RUNCORN. Sir,—Mv opinion having been asked as to the legality of the appointment on the Library Committee which was made by the Commissioners at their last meeting. I would direct attention to one of the standing orders of the Board which reads as follows That every vacancy in any committee, or in any office under tha Board, shall be noti- fied to the Board at their monthly meeting next after such vacancy, and shall be filled up at the following monthly meeting of the Board." As the resignation was only re- ceived that day, it is clear the appointment is not in accor- dance with the above-named Standing Order, and it is sur- prising to some that so little attention is paid by the officials of the Board and many of the Commissioners to the Stand- ing Orders which are supposed to be the guide for conduct -of business. One member congratulated them upon the quick way in which they had got through their business. In my view there is greater merit in doing business correctly and well than in doing it in a hurry-scurry, slip-shod fashion. Yours truly, VERITY. RUBCOIII, May 25th, 1887.

THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—l think we may now safely conclude that the freeing of the Lending Library will be part of the Jubilee celebra- tion in Warrington. Every member of the Museum and Library Committee is favourable to the project—for they have often told /19 so themselves, and they are, to use Marc Antony's phrase, all " honourable men "—and ,the only thing that prevented them from giving effect, so far as they were concerned, to their strong private incline- ' Cons to free the Library,was that, on looking a little ahead, as became judicions stewards of a public institution, they were afraid that the money at their disposal would not enable them to do so. What hindered them from admitting to the fullest benefit of the Library even the poorest inhabi- tant of Warrington was the fear of a deficit and nothing wore. This fear removed, and their ardour for a real free library would be more irrepressible than that of the most captious of their critics. 'lbis was the position taken up by the Museum and Library Committee, and it is because this was their position that I think we may congratulate ourselves that the freeing of the Library will be an accom- plished fact before the year is out. The noble offer of Mr. Morris to make good any deficit that may occur during the next five years has removed the fear of the Library Com- mittee, and as that was the only barrier that stood between us and a free library, surelry it is only logical to conclude that the Library is as good as free.

div.p: URBICUS.

WARRINGTON AND THE JUBILEE. Sir,—l should feel glad if you could find space in your valuable paper for a few observations on "S. D.'s" letter. First let me say I object to "S. D.'s" very unwise and an- jest reference to Mr. Crosfield's very kind gift to a hard- working class who seldom get recognised as they deserve. It shows very bad taste on his part to mention the political touch. I say it is unwise and unjust, seeing the offer is to all creeds and denominations. Of course we know anything coming from Mr. Crosfield would be "a political dodge" in "S. D.'s " eyes; but I would ask him what he thinks of Sir Gilbert's gift to the churches, when placed along side of Mr Crosfield's generous gift to all alike ? But my sympathy goes out to those poor children who are too poor to attend any Sunday school, and I can't think why they should be left out of a national 'esti rat. I say L. will be a shame if they are not looked after, but as Sunday schools we shall have enough to do to discipline our own scholars, and is my only object in writing this letter i 3 to see if something cannot be cone for them. It is a fine op- portunity for those gentlemen who look upon our Sunday schoole with disdain to come forward and show their charity. I should say "S. D." could easily provide for 500 of them, and there are many more in his position who could do the same, and I should be the last to say it was a political dodge. I do hope something will be done for them, and make it a real Jubilee to all the children. A SUNDAY SCHOOLTEACHER. Warrington, May 26, 1887.

EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON AND THE JUBILEE. Sir,—l read your account of the Jubilee proposals for Newton and Earlestown with some intereat last week. I was glad te sea some names not usually associated with Sunday school work, and sorry to see others omitted that , are so associated, but all present at the meeting united in their desire to make the celebration of the Queen's Jubilee worthy of the occasion in Newton and Earlestown. For I take it that both the day and Sunday school scholars are included in the estimated number of 3,000. If they are not so included, both old and young, it will lose half its importance in this neighbourhood. No one that I have met with has anything to say against Dr. Mouncey's proposal for a Cottage Hospital either, which on all hands is admitted to be a desirable thing of itself if attainable. I dare say it will be found on inquiry that the Railway Company are subscribers to the hospitals in Liverpool, and perhaps Manchester, and that they have facilities of conveyance to those places not pos- sessed by the general public. The other places mentioned are more or less interested in them also. It cannot have escaped notice that many cases have been sent there for the sake of obtaining special treatment by specialists, but hav- ing said this I am free to add my testimony that many cases would be infinitely better dealt with in such a Cot- tage Hospital as has been suggested, than in the distrac- tions of many homes with no provision for accident or sick. uses. Hitherto we have looked I. the Railway Company to Initiate such things; will they take this matter up, or if taken up by others will they support it? These twe things do not by any means exhaust the list of things desirable to be had in Earlestown—public baths, a public hall, these must be left to private enterprise for reasons best known to the initiated. But if we can get a Recreation Ground that shall not be an incubus and lasting burthen, that will surely be an instalment of good things. It savours to me of look- ing a gift horse in the mouth to see how old it is—after the hopeful way in which Mr. Pardy spoke of being able to approach Mr Legh on the subject of the Recreation Ground. As long as we keep to the highways we may roam as far as we like, but the moment we step on to any green spot of earth hereabouts we place ourselves in jeopardy.—Yours truly,

div.head: EARLESTONIAN.
div.p: EARLESTONIAN.

THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS. Sir,—Your correspondent "X" asks several questions Twill try te answer. The Liberal Unionists are not doing, or in- clined to do anything of which they will be ashamed. We deny that we have deserted the Liberal party, or deserted our leader, or run counter to our life-long political profes- sion. We are consistent Liberals, and shall neither be bribed by the best robes, nor coerced by intolerance into accepting a Policy dictated solely by Mr. Gladstone. and opposed, as we believe, to the best interests of the country. When and bow have the Liberal party been consulted in the Gladstone-Parnellite policy ? Will "X" say by what authority he and his friends claim to be right, and all these who differ from them necessarily wrong in this matter ? We do not condemn them who honestly differ, or assume that the truth of this matter rests with us. We are all bound to exercise our judgment, and to act accordingly,and no man or party has a right to assume an authority over its members in such a matter when it has not been con- sulted. It will be time enough for " X "and his friends to give their sympathy when asked. If he will look to the broken ranks of the Liberal party, with a solid majority of over 100 against them, they have little to boast of. A little more courtesy in speaking of opponents would not be unbee coming, and lam not aware that we are ." herding with swine or feeding upon husks." Our Conservative fellow townsmen, who differ from us as to the policy of govern- ment, don't deserve such a name, arid you may depend upon it such language does the Liberal party no goad. There is too much condemnation of those who differ from us in poli- tical matters. Less of it, and a greater desire to see the truth as it really is, would give the Liberal party a greater hold of Liberals than it possesses at present, and things are not so perfect in the Liberal ranks that no reforms are re- quired. We see no desire to game to rl mutual understanding as to the policy for Ireland, or any real desire for re-union except by our unconditionally accepting the Gladstone- Parnellite demands. We do see a determination to persist in these demands, and to force them upon the country by party agitation and organisation, and it will be our duty to defeat this, if we can. In doing so we are not deserting Liberalism ; we are following the lead of well tried veterans in the Liberal ranks, men who have dons good service to the party when Mr. Gladstone retired in disgust from it, because the country then declined to follow his lead, as it does to-day.—Yours truly,

div.head: F. MONKS.
div.p: F. MONKS.

THE IRISH QUESTION. Sir,—l see from your news column that an attempt is being made to form a Liberal Unionist Association in War- rington. I suppose the idea has originated in the fart brain of one of the conscience-stricken Liberals, who, with Lord Ilartington, dreads that "sound Liberals " insanely etaamoured of a paper union "would have no alternative but to separate themselves definitely from their party and join the ranks of the Conservatives." I would advise these so•called Uaionists to reckon themselves up a little and see how mucn they are worth. In the first place they are very much like what the Parnellites were until recently; they are acting as "pudding in the childish game of see saw " —which-ever way they lean down comes the plank. Again, is it not clear to the Unionists that the Irish mem- bers were, previous to Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, the sole legislators for the Empire, having at their feet the two political parties? Do they want this to continue? Is it possible for an independent legislature to exist with a national party in its midst determined to make all the poli- tical machinery subservient to its own views and ends? Certainly not, and only in the brains of political Don Quioates could such an idea rind a lodgement. I do not care at the present time to call up spirits from the vasty deep, in the form of extracts from the political speeches of our whilom political educators—John Bright and Joseph Chamberlain. It is sufficient to feel, that hav- ing edecated na to know that our thorough and almost complete system of Political representation has but one logical and economical outcome, viz,—self-government, theSe two gentlemen have thrown their teachings and their party overboard, at the bidding of a party which has not one single honest conviction, nor yet a tradition to which thew can look back to with anything else but shame. JOHN GORDON McMINNIES ON HIS SEVENTIETH BIRTHDAY. Here's a health to the Captain beloved by his crew, And we gladly our fond tribute pay, While we wish him, with hearts ever loyal and, true, "Many happy returns of the day." 0, he fears not the tempest—his heart never failed— And he faces the foe with a will. It is long, long ago since his colours were nailed To the mast, and they're flying there still. He has fought for the right as a stout Captain should, With an earnest and generous mind. With a hand ever helping in all that is good, He has laboured to better his kind. He has grown gray in service, and grown the more dear, For his heart is as fresh as the May; May he still live to lead us for many a year— " Many happy returns of the day.' Warrington, May 27, 1887.
-ED. Ex.
A RAILWAY MYSTERY.

A mysterious affair has this week occurred on the London and North-Western Railway near Warring- ton. A deep sea pilot named H. J. Leming, who be- longs to Dover, and who, it is said, had piloted a vessel to a port on the e .st coast of Scotland, com- menced his return journey south, and joined the limited mail at Perth on Monday. When he left that station the only other occupant of the com- partment of the third class carriage in which he was seated was a sailor, who, it has been ascer- tained, was going to Cardiff. Leming fell asleep. At 11-30 at night the train arrived a. Bank Quay Station, Warrington, where the usual transfer of mails took place. The nest stopping place was at Crewe, but at Norton crossing, about three miles from Warrington, Leming is supposed to have either fallen out of the train, or to t ave been pushed out, when it was going at the rate of close upon fifty miles an hour. He remainedwhere he fell until day- light on Tuesday morning, when he managed to crawl to a signalman's hut in the neighbourhood, where he told the strange story above narrated. A tele- gram was despatched to the stationmaster at War- rington, who at once sent down an engine and car- riage. In the meantime word was conveyed to the infirmary, and Dr. Smith was waiting at the station ready to render assistance when the injured man arrived. A cab was also in waiting. and Leming was taken to the Infirmary. There it was found that one of his ribs was broken, and that he was cut and bruised. On being questioned, he said 'that his money was all right, and displayed it in a belt, where it was secured. He refused to remain in the hospital, and the same afternoon he took train to London. It is not known how he came to fall from the train, but the railway authorities are making inquiries into the matter. He was not, so far as can be learned, noticed in the train at Warrington, and it is supposed that he was still sleeping.
The whole of the miners employed atVauxhall Collieries, Ituabon. North Wales, have struck work owine to a wages dispute with the coal owners. Several hundred men are thus thrown out of work.

The premises occupied by Messrs. Medina, mattrass makers, at Bow, were destroyed by fire on Thursday. The tunes also spread to the railway arches adjoining. and to a woodvardt the darnage being great. At the annual meeting in London, on Thursday, of the Iron and Steel Institute, the newly-elected President, Mr. D. Adamson, of Manchester, took the chair, and delivered his his presidential address, which dealt with the properties of iron and steel. .

..„.. MR. GLADSTONE AT Holm—Mr. Gladstone, accom- panied by Mrs Gladstone, who travelled by the ten train from Willesden on Thursday morning, reached Chester General Railway Station at ten minutes to three o'clock in the afternoon. They retched the Castle shortly before four o'clock, driving home from Chester. THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY —The Prime Minieter gave a State dinner to the Foreign Ambassadors and others on Tuesday night in celebration of the Queen's birthday. Among the guests was the Prince of Wares. Official dinners were also given by Mr. Stanhope, Mr. Goschen, Lord Cross, Lord George Hamilton, and Mr. H. Mathews. QUITE RIGHT.—In refusing to approve of a composition of 2s 6d in the pound offered by a Bury bankrupt, the Judge of the Bolton County Court (Mr. Brynmor Jones) said that a man in bankruptcy ought not to be whitewashed simply because his creditors had met together and were willing to accept whatever proposal he might make. DEATH OF TILE EARL OF MEATH. On Thursday the Earl of Meath died at his residence, Kilruddery, near Bray, aged 84. He was Lord Lieutenant of county Wicklow, and honorary colonelof the Dublin Fusiliers. As Lord Braba- zon he sat in Parliament for county Dublin from 1837 to to 1841. He was a member of the Irish Lights Board, and chairman of different boards. He is succeeded in the title by his son, Begiiiald Lord Brabaacin. BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—At the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday, a widow named Noon, 37 years old, with three children, brought an action against a man named Veevers, aged 51, who, though a widower when he was courting the plaintiff, WAS now married to a woman with a public-house and six children. The jury awarded the plaintiff £BO. The circumstances of the case caused Mr. Justice Wills to remark that some people thought such ac- tions ought to be abolished, bat for his part he thought women should hr. a this means of protection against men playing with them. SUPPOSED DYNAMITARDS IN A HOLYHEAD TRAIN.—A. foreman platelaver on the Chester and Holyhead line was walking along the railway en Wednesday, near Flint Sta- tion, when he found three cartridges, each about five inches long, together with a tin box about six inches long. The lid of the box was off, and it bad a small hole drilled in the side as if for insertion of a time fuse. Upon examination the three cartridges were found to be 'full of dynamite. The stuff is in possession of the railway authorities, and a thorough investigation is being made into the matter. The supposition is that the whole apparatus had been thrown upon the railway from a passing express train. C )LLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR WIGAN. -THREE LIVES LOST.

An explosion occurred at eight o'clock on Thurs- day night, at Lilly Lane Colliery, Bryn, near Wigan. The night shift consisted of about nine men. A blast of wind knocked them down, rendering them insensible. An alarm being raised, Mr. Isaac James, manager, and Mr. Grimble, mining engineer, descended with a party, and, according to the best information obtainable, found one man, John Lowe, dead. Two others, John Harrison and. Peter Clare, are undiscovered, with little hope of rescue. Four others were brought up suffering from as and bruises. The explosion was felt at Edgehill Col- liery, which communicates with Lilly Leine, a mile distant. . .

Another report says :—An alarming explosion oc- curred on Thursday night at Lilly-lane Colliery, Bryn, near Wigan, by which several lives are be • lieved to have been lost. The colliery, which is owned by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., employs about 150 men and boys, and the usual number were working up to 4 p.m. When the hands came up all appeared right. The night shift went down an hour later, including Joseph Houlton, foreman; George Prescott, furnaceman ; and John Hamson, John Lowe, James Lowe, Peter Clare, John Ryan, and John Gourley, all furnacemen. From the statement of Ryan, who lives at Gol- borne, the following particulars have been gathered :—"At eight o'clock we felt a blast of wind, which took me and my mate of our feet. We were carried about a dozen yards and knocked down insensible. As soon as I recovered conscious- ness I got to the shaft, and was taken to the sur- face." Ryan, whose head was severely cut, pro- ceeded home. Other information shows that about eight o'clock the engineman noticed an unusual "puff " coming up the shaft, and at once raised an alarm. At five o'clock on Friday morning Isaac James, manager, and Richd.Potter, underlooker, after being in the workings nearly nine hours, were brought up in an almost senseless condition owing to their pro- longed search and the poisonous afterdamp. These brave fellows, accompanied by the general manager, Mr. B. B. Glover, risked their lives in the attempt to rescue the two, men, Peter Clare and John Harrison, who were missing. The exploring party found the main road entirely blocked by a large fall of roof. An attempt was made to enter the workings by the Edge Green pit, a mile away, but this road, too, was blocked, 'The dead body of John Lowe, a married man, of Edge Green, was found between the pit eye I and the fall of the roof. Several doctors were early I in attendance, in the hope of rendering assistance to the missing men. The ghastly preparations for the reception of the I dead were being carried on on FridapafternOn. Knots of women and children gathered round the pit's, mouth, the children looking wistfully into their mother's eyes, realising the solemnity of the scene. An incident occurred which buoyed the hopes for a moment. A little trapper boy came up from the pit with lamp in hand, who was received with expectant eyes. He came but to tell that the poor fellows were not yet discovered, the workings being completely blocked. One poor woman awaited her hdsband, believing, to use her own words, "God would save Jim." The sight was indeed.heartrend- sing, and the fortitude with which the poor creatures bore the scene was most impressive. The death roll numbers three, all shot lighters, who were down the pit performing their accus- tomed task, which has now to be done while the general body of workmen are out of the mine. The accident occurred in the 'Wigan 9:t., the scene of so many previous explosions. Only one body has yet been recovered, the explorers up to noon not having been able to discover the other two, who are sup- posed to be buried by falls of the roof, which are numerous and heavy. The chokedamp met with has been very powerful, and many of the explorers have had to be carried out of the workings and medically attended. The injured men were visited on Friday morning by the doctor, and all are re- ported to be progressing as favourably as corld be expected.

speech "that the policy of the Liberal party for the last 20 years, had converted the statute book into a facsimile of the "Newgate Calendar" Do the Unionists, who are now under the same umbrella with this wiseacre, believe this? This land-owning turllte says" the Liberals signalised their tenure of office by a series of legislative robberies." Now, I ; know Unionists will pooh-pooh this man's name and very likely call him a fool. If they said the same of his political acquaintances generally,l should not object. None the less the Tory party believe, or say tbe same thing What lam interested in is to know where the robbery comes in. Let us take Colonel King-Harman, a shining light just now for Liberal Unionists. From being convicted of riotous and disorderly conduct at the gardens of Cremorne, be de- veloped into a Home Euler. Preferment, of course, was out of the question amongst men of brains like the leaders of the Home Rule party, so the colonel threw in his lot with John Bright's friends, the "stupid party." As a landowner, he refused to reduce his rents until the land commissioners compelled him; and on the Longford estates this was done to the tnee of 50 per cent. His rental, be- fore the reduction, amounted to £42.662. Accerding to "Jimmy Lowther," it is "legislative robbery" to step this Irish place-hunter from robbing the Irish farmer, and, what is worst of all, and what makes one almost despair of seeing a better state of things, is that men who know all this and look to the land question as containing the secret of all our troubles, are now working to keep it a party who are content to keep place and its privileges, not caring one toss whether "Joseph and his brethren" or the heir to a dukedom dictate the conditions or not. I have no doubt a fellow feeling amongst a certain class of capitalists for their land-owning allies helps wonderfully to cement the Unionists together, but how, in the name of all theta wonderful. working-men are to be found willing to work shoulder to shoulder with the classes, passes my com- prehension. English working-men helping English dukes to squeeze Irish farmers ! In the "New Doomsday Book" I find that the non- resident land owners in Ireland number 1,643, and that these bold 4,513,861 acres, with a valuation of £2,139,143 It is computed that the total rental taken from the country and spent elsewhere amounts to at least £5,000.000 a year., The noble Cavendishes must have many a secret laugh over the gullibility of Enelieh working-men as they pocket their yearly rental of £189,380. With a rental like this they can afford to put off all those other questions that have been brought about and are continuing the trade depression. If these coroneted vampires dangle "integrity of the Empire" before our eyes, of course it is our duty to fall down and worship, and some of us do it; the reward will come by and by. Working-men should know that when employers break off from old associations that there are wheels within wheels and private ends te be gained sufficiently significant to forbid any help being given by their class. It only remains to say how great a mystery it is that any man can be influenced by the kind of literature now being spread by the Unionists. Sensational in its character, it is utterly unreliable,and is little short of being as cowardly as the "Times and the Government have just proved to be. The "Times" WAS never a friend of the people ; to the Irish patriots it has always been a malignant enemy. O'Connell was thus assailed in the " Times "

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 28, 1887. i,ATEST NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 28, 1887. i,ATEST NEWS.

„ The Prince of Wales has accepted the poet of honorary president of the Glasgow Exhibition. At Bootle, on Friday, James Henry Callan, headmaster of St. James Roman Catholic School, was fined 103 and costs for ill-using l'avid Ford, a scholar, aged twelve. In the Queen's Bench Division, on Friday, Henry Saun- ders, a Wolverhampton solicitor, was ordered to be struck off the rolls for having appropriated client's money. The eviction at Bodyke, Ireland, were commenced on Friday morning, but it bad to be abandoned in consequence of the sub-sheriff being seized with an apopletic fit. At the Old Bailey, on Friday, Dr. Phillip Sale, managing director of Protector Cattle and Carriage Insurance, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for obtaining money 1 by fraud. Owing to the position taken up by tbe Earl of Sefton in regard to the letting of the ground at Micas, the projected review and sham fight of the volunteers ea Monday next has had to be abandoned. TERRIBLE DEATH BY SCALDINCL—A man named John Thompson, employed at the Spring-lane Brewery, Sheffield, died in the hospital on Friday morning, after terrible suffer- ing, from scalds. He fell on Thursday afternoon into a tank of boiling water, and his whole body MRS immersed except his head and face. LORD COLIN CAMPBELL'S BANKRUPTCY —At the Lon- don Bankruptcy Court, on Friday. Lord Colin Campbell attended before the Chief Official Receiver, and consented to adjudication. lie said he had no residence of his own in London. His unsecured liabilities, exclusive of costs, reached £3,600, and his costs about £6,000. VaA FLOODED COLLIERY: THREE MEN DROWNED.—On Friday a collier, in Tunshill Pit, Milner-row, near Rochdale, struck into a disused pit full of water, causing an inrush which imperilled the lives of over 100 men. The pit was completely flooded, and three men were drowned. The escape of the others is considered marvellous. Sam:ma° • BarrrEEß. At the Central Criminal Court, on Friday, Wm. Holt Brandt, aged 20, was charged with the murder of his brother, Thomas, by shooting him with a revolver at Dulwich on the night of the sth May. In the end the jury acquitted on the ground of insanity, sod he was ordered to ha detained during her Majesty's

pleasure. FATAL FIRE AT AN ASYLLTIL—On Friday afternoon a fire was discovered upon the premises of Dr. Adams's private lunatic asylum, Clapton, London, in which some 250 pa- tients are under treatment. Hours elapsed before the fire was extinguished, and not then until great damage was done. The body of Mrs Valiance was burned to a cinder ; but the lunatics were removed to a place of safety. THE TITHE WAR IN WALES.—The parish of Meifod, ' Montgomeryshire, was all astir as early as six o'clock on Friday morning in anticipation of the sales on the six farms distrained upon by the representatives of the Dean and Chapter of Christ Church, Oxford. A crowd had collected and formai themselves in strong force on an embankment, and as the police came up the mob fell on them with sticks, and a scene of wild disorder ensued. A farmer was knocked down by the police, and another farmer was torn from his horse. The greatest confusion prevailed.

IMPURE PEPPER AT WIDNES. Before Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. A. Fletcher, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Elijah Withington, mana- ger of a branch shop at Simm's Cross, Widnes, belonging to the Runcorn Co-operative Society, was summoned for sell- ing pepper which was not of the substance and quality ; demanded.—The certificate of the county analyst stated there was 10 per cent of adulteration. The impurity was ground olive stones. The defendant pleaded guilty, and he was lined 404 and costs. He stated that the committee of managetnent always purchased the pepper on the under- standing that it was pure.—Messrs. Charles Flynn and Wm. Snodden, grocers, of Ant 3treet, were also summoned on a similar charge. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defen- dants. The analyst's certificate stated that there was 4 per cent of impurity in the sample of pepper. Ground olive stones was the adulterative material.—Mr. Swift said his clients purchased the pepper from a middleman who was himself a grocer, and the latter had a written guarantee from the grinders of its absolute purity. He asked the magistrates to exercise the power vested in them, and send a sample of the pepper for analysis to Somerset House.—Mr. Gaskell : We are quite aware of our powers, ant we shall not act upon them.—Mr. Swift : Will your worships grant an adjournment to enable as to have it sent —Mr. Gaskell: Yoe eoll send it after- wards.—Mr. Swift: That will t s of no avail after your worships have fined the defendants.—Mr. Gaskell : You can appeal.—Mr. Swift said Mr. Campbell Brown had made mistakes before, and he had reason to think he was not cor- rect in this matter. It was a well known fact that Mr. Brown did not always make the analysis himself. He added that a sample of the pepper was now in process of analysis by Mr. Hughes, of Liverpool, and asked for an ad- joarnmeet.—Mr. Spencely (the clerk) said his certificate would not settle the matter.—Mr. Swift: And my sugges- tion is that Campbell Brown is not gospel.—Mr. Gaskell : We think the case had better go on ; we think there is nothing to be gained by delay.—Mr. Swift said the amount of adulteration which was certified was so absurdly small- -4 per cent—that it struck him no man in his senses would thick of incorporating it into pure pepper.—Mr.Gaskell : The amount of adulteration is small, and we shall take that fact into consideration, and therefore fine the defendants 20s and costs.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN NEW YORK.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN NEW YORK.

- _ An alarming fire broke out at two o'clock en Friday morning in the stables owned by the Street Car Company. in Tenth-avenue, New York. So rapidly did the fire spread that it is feared many had fallen victims before they could be aroused or rescued. The stables were entirely gutted, and the Tenth.avenue was destroyed from Fifty-fourth- street. The fire spread to fifty-third and fifty-second streets, end the Eleventh-avenue burned fiercely. Sixteen hundred horses parished in the flames, and the loss is cer- tainly not less than £1,000,000. NEW YORE, FRIDAY, 5 AlR.—The fire continues to spread, all efforts to check it having 89 far failed. It is re. ported that a large number of persons have lost their lives, but it is impossible to verify this in the present excitement and confusion. The pecuniary loss will be much greater than was at first reported. THE PARIS CATASTROPHE.-226 PERSONS KILLED A,ND INJURED.

..----- _ _ Paws, FRIDAY.—The searching for bodies among the ruins of the op6ra Comique, which was suspended last night and was resumed this morning, will now continue without interruption. The work by niaht will be conduc- ted by the aid of the electric light. It is stated that twenty bodies of the spectators who were suffocated have been found lying in a heap in the refreshment room of the theatre. The firemen also saw other bodies which they have not been able to reach. The " Voltaire " 19 of opinion that no fewer than 150 bodies lie buried beneath the ruins.

The "Globe" pablishes the following telegram from Paris, dated this morning :—The "Garlic's' now states that 226 persons are already known to have been either killed or injured in the fire at the Opera COrnique. Fifty- eight dead bodies have been brought out of the ruins, thirty persons have been seriously injured, and sixty have sus- tained injuries of a more or less serious character. In ad- dition to these one hundred persons are missing, and there is little doubt that their remains lie buried beneath the debris of the theatre. The greatest excitement continues to prevail, and most lamentable scenes are being witnessed.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were pre- sent the Revs J W N Tanner and J Lockwood; Messrs Mclntyre, Lewis, Aaron, Stokes, Brandreth, Hall, Parr, Hid- field, Wallington, Hamilton, Fairhurst, Turner, Warburton, Percival, H Linaker (clerk), and W H Linaker (deputy clerk). .

- THE MEDICAL OFFICER.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board, who signified their approval of the re-appointment of Dr. Adams as medical officer for the ensu- ing 12 months at a salary of £l2O per annum. Tun COUNTY Awelss.r.—Mr Farrington said, as requested at the last meeting, he had written to the county analyst with regard to the water supply of Appleton Thorn New Vicarage. He had submitted the analysis at the last meet- ing, and as it was considered rather vague he had written to ask if the water was fit for domestic use. This was the re- ply :—" Society 'Chemical Industry, Manchester section, May 23rd, 1887.—Dear Sir,—l do not consider No. 220 a first-class water, but if you are certain that no sewage is finding its way into the water, then I should say that it is fit for domestlc purposes. Many towns, such as Northwich, are supplied with water of this quality.—l remain, yours truly, J. CARTER BELL."—Mr Aaron: I shoulei see that no more water went to that gentleman to be analysed.—Mr Brandreth : But he gets £3OO a year from the county for analysing.—Mr Aaron : And we have to pay him for every sample.—Mr Brandreth : Yes; we have to pay 76 6d per sample beside.--The Deputy Clerk: No; it is 6s per earn- pie—Mr Aaron : I make a proposition that be be written to to give a proper analysis of the water. He save" if there is no sewage going in, it is good water ! "—Mr Hadfield: You could say that.—Mr Aaron : Of course.—Mr Wallington: I think it is for the analyst to say whether any sewage goes '; into the water.—The Clerk (to Inspector): Have you got 1 the analysis with you 7—lnspector Farrington : I have not. —Mr Hadfield: He has analysed the water then 7—Mr ' Aaron : But be does not tell us what is in it. He says it is "fair water." He is like a good many more chemists; he will guess and put it down.-1 he Chairman instructed the !, Inspector to bring the analysis with him at the next meet. ling, and the Authority could then decide what should be ; dose. There was no other business of interest.

div.head: ST. HELENS GROCER AND MS WIDNES CUSTOMER.
div.p: A ST. HELENS GROCER AND MS WIDNES CUSTOMER.

On Thursday at Widoes Petty Sessions, before Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. A. Fletcher, Sarah Connolly, grocer, Crow Wood, Widnes, was summoned on a charge of obtain- ing by false pretences from William Howard, wholesale grocer, Church•s'reet, St. Helens, goods of the value of £l3 Os 101—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the prosecution, and the defendant was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles. —From the statement of Mr. Riley, it appeared that the defendant owed Mr. Howard about £7O on account of various business transactions. She, however, gave an order for a further supply of goods, and as they did • not arrive at the expected time she went over to St. Helens. In Mr. Howard's shop she found the complainant and Mr. Kirk- ham, a collector of debts. During a conversation which took place in a sitting•room behind the shop, she was told that, unless she was prepared to make a substan- tial cash payment of front £2O to £3O, or gave security she could not have the goods. She replied that a cash pay- ment was impossible, and a similar answer was made to the suggestion of a bill of sale. She, however, said she would give an assignment of a share she bad under her father's will. She alleged that when her father died he left every- thing to her mother for life, and had then to be divided amongst seven children. She went into particulars of the estate, arriving at the conclusion that it was worth £7OO, and her share would be £lOO. As Mrs. Connolly wanted the goods particularly on that day, as the shop would have to be " stopped " if she did not get them, Mr. Kirkham at once instructed Mr. Howard's solicitor to prepare an assign- ment of her share in her father's (the late Richard Barkers estate. On the strength of this the goods were sent to her. A few weeks later Mr. Howard, being in Liverpool, went to the probate registry, and found that Mrs. Connolly had no interest whatever under her father's will, as all the real and personal estate was assigned to her mother and her heirs ateolntely.—Mr. Knowles pointed out that Mrs Connolly had paid to the complainant about ZS on account of the goods, thus showing that it was an ordinary creditor and debtor matter of business, and not a criminal transaction It was simply a matter for a civil court.—Mr. Riley replied that it was in civil transactions where false pretences did arise. lie thought the Bench would be advised that if she had paid for the whole of the goods it would be perfectly immaterial to the point in tke view of the law.—The Bench decided that the case must go on.— William Joseph K‘rkham, auctioneer and accountant, St. Helens, gave evidence bearing out Mr. Riley's opening statement.—The complainant was then called, and admitted that he was not present at the interview when the arrange- ment was agreed upon. Mr. Kirkham told him of the re- sult of the conversation. He authorised the delivery of the goods before she gave the assignment. If he had not be- lieved that she had an interest in her father's will he should not have allowed the goods to go.—The Beech considered that upon this evidence the case would fall to the ground.— Mr. Riley said he would, therefore, take the responsibility of not calling any further witnesses, and having regard to the sex of the defendant he thought it would searcely be right, to endeavour to reason their worships out of their con- viction on the facts. Their worshipti considered the facts Were not sufficient to warrant the committal of the , woman ? Mr. Gaskell : Yes.— The defendant was then I allowed to depart.

A QUARREL BETWEEN RUNCORN TRADESMEN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Messrs. C. Reynolds and G. L. Davies, Charles Herbert Cook, ap- parently about 9 years of age, was charged with assaulting Sarah Hopley. Thomas Cook, shoemaker, Church-street, father of the boy, was charged with causing the boy to commit the assault. There was a cross-summons charging Sarah Elopley with assaulting Charles Herbert Cook. Mr. F. A. Lake represented Hopley, and the defendants Cook were defended by Mr. Burton. From Mr. Lake's opening statement it appeared that Hanley is a domestic servant in the employ of Mr. S. Yarwood, cab proprietor, Church-st., and Mr. Cook was a neighbour of the latter. Their back premises were connected by a passage with Brunswick-st., and the gate leading out of this passage iota Mr. Yarwood's yard was about three or four feet 'from the back yard gate of Mr. Cook's house. Unfortunately these people had not lived on the most neighbourly terms, and it was merely through this want of neighbourly spirit that these snm• monses bad arisen. For some time past MY. Yarwood had complained of his yard being scattered over with all kinds of filthy refuse. On Thursday last Sarah Hopley *as swilling the yard of Mr. Yarwood's house, and whilst she was doing so. somebody from the other side of the gate tbruat into the yard leather scrapings, feathers, and other filth, so that as fast as the girl cleaned, the yard it was dirtied again. The girl complained to Mr. Yarwood, who went up into a bedroom commanding a view of the premises. He saw Mr. and Mrs Cook and the infant de- fendant standing quietly at the gate waiting for the door to be opened and immediately this was done Mr. Cook urged the bey to strike her with a brush he carried. The boy obeyed his father and struck Honley a blow on the shoulder that caused her pain all day. The father and son immedi- ately returned into the house, and Mr. Yar- wood went to make a complaint of this conduct, and to ask for an apology. Mr. Cook, however, would not open the door, but shouted through the key hole " Thee go away, or else I'll summon thee again."—ln de- fence, Mr. Burton called Charles Herbert Cook, who said water was flowing inro the middle of his father's yard, and he brushed it back. Henley then opened the door of Mr. Yarwood's back yard, and threw some water on his legs. He had then the brush on his shoulder, and let it fall, but he did not strike Hopley, nor did the brush come in contact with her.—ln answer to Mr. Lake the witness said he had not talked over the affair with his Lake, but his father had told him whatever I said I must not alter it. (Laughter.)— Mr. Lake: Therefore, haying said you did not strike Hop- ley, you must not now say that you did.—The Boy: No, sir.—That would be against your father's instructions? Yes..—Lena Snelson, servant to Mr. Cook, corroborated the boy's statement -Miss Mary Jane Cook denied that any blow was struck, but said she beard Mrs. Yarwood say to Hopley "Why did not you give him a crack on the nose with the brush." She was at the " landing " window at this time. —Thomas Cook, the defendant, said from what his wife said he went into the yard, which was all wet, and be fetched his boy in. He never saw any blows struck. There was

not any necessity for the water from Mr, Yarwood's yard to flow into his, No one, to hie knowledge, had thrown ref use into Mr. Yarwood's yard. It was untrue that he tol d the boy "to go at" Hopley.—ln reply to Mr. Lake, witness denied all the evidence for the complainant. He ad mitted that he went to Hopley's house, and said it would be well if they could come to an agreement, as he did not want to go into court.—Mr. Cook having been examined, Mr. Burton addressed tbe Bench, and Mr. Yarwood and Sarah Hopley were re-called.—The Bench dismissed all three summonses, Mr. Reynolds remarking that it was a great pity that such a case should have been brought into court. Mr. Lake and Mr. Barton concurred in that opinion.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES —At a meeting of the Frod- sham and Frodshem Lordship Parochial Committees, held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday evening, Mr. A. Thomas in the chair, the Clerk reported that he had, in accordance with instructions received at a previous meeting, had an interview with Mr Houndall, one of the officials of the Local Government Board at Whitehall, and explained to him the present position of the Authority with respect to the loans to be borrowed for the Frodsham water scheme, and referred to the quantity of water per head per day, viz, 20 gallons, mentioned in General Carey's repot t as being ex- cessive, and that the Authority believed the Newton scheme, as proposed by Mr. Bancroft, was sufficient. Mr. Bancroft, the engineer, being in town, offered to give any further in- formation, and accompanied the Clerk to Whitehall. Mr. Houndall having expressed a desire to see the engineer, Mr. Bancroft was called up and fully explained the Newton scheme, and what he would have liked to do in making edits. Mr. Houndall finally said that if the Authority would put the case before the Local Government Board, and Mr. Bancroft explain the above in detail, and the whole of the money expended could be brought into the scheme, a fur. ther amount to fully test, &c, might be obtained, and the loan be sanctioned for the time asked W.—After a long dis- cussion, it was resolved that Mr Bancroft be asked en what terms he will furnish a special report on the scheme for supplying water to Frodsham, to furnish to the Local Go. vernment Board.—Tbe Inspector of Nuisances reported that he had ascertained the depth and condition of the road drain in Kingsley-rd„Overton,and produced a tender from Mr. J. Littler for carrying out the necessary workin extending the drain in question, which amounted to £l2 17s. Resolved that Mr. Littler's tender be accepted, the works to be com- pleted as early as possible.—The Inspector further reported that the tank at the sewage outfall works near Helsby required emptying, and that the sewage works generally had ben very much damaged and trespassed upon. He was directed te have the tank cleansed and emptied forth- with.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDEWn 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The Stock Exchange has been occupied almost entirely 4 with the settlement, and near approach of another holiday limits business. Prices, however, are well maintained, and holders take care to keep them for the present. Some of the better classes of foreigners, and home rail- ways especially, are being held, more with a view to secur- ing the large margin of profit between the rates they yield and the present price of money. The next dividend period being now only three months off, it is not apprehended that money will get much dearer before then. By paying for three months the very moderate contangees now charged, specu- lative buyers have a fair chance of being able to make a turn out of the dividends as well as out of the stocks. A sudden rise in the value of money would, of course, upset such calculations, and compel holders to get out sooner than they bad intended. Cheap money benefits non•dividend stocks in a differeet way. They are being taken up not, of course, for what they yield, but in order to lighten contangoes, and reduce the appearance of pretty large scale in Mexican' Railway. A good deal of ordinary and second Preference has been put in pawn for the purpose of making an easy carry over. This, combined with the favourable traffic, induced BOMB buy- ing for the new account, and gave them a show of firm. nese. Tnere is still a brisk demand for certain classes of gold miles, the cortinued rise in two or three companies giving an impetus to most. The well known character of the Transvaal as a gold producing country is daily becoming I recognised, and anything connected with it is almost cer- tain to go. The Hotel du Nord has declared a dividend at the rate of 8 per cent per annum, and have made an issue of the bal. ance of the unallotted capital, which is six thousand shares of £lO each. Cologne has made such progress that it has become one of the most important cities of Germany as a I business centre, and its unique position on the Rhine I renders it a place of attraction to every class of visitor. Railway traffic returns for the past week are, on the whole, very favourable, the good lines especially showing con- siderable increase. There is an active demand for certain classes of miscellaneous shares, Guinness loading the way with a nominal rise of 10.

div.head: RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. – • – – – – – –
div.p: RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. - • - - - - - -

The arrangements for the celet-Tration of the Queen's Ju- bilee are progressing apace. A week ago a difficulty had arisen that it was thought would imperil the successful carrying out of the demonstration resolved upon. The church party claimed as a right that the children represert, ting their schools should take precedence in the processions that were to be organised in honour of the Queen's long reign, because they were a branch of the State Church. The Nonconformists on the somewhat unwieldy committee that had been appointed, argued that the order of the pro- cession should be exactly in relation to the date of the establishment of the schools. While the representatives of the latter body were quite willing that the meeting should decide the question—and the opinion of the Noncon- formists was not undivided—the delegates of the Establish- ment were not at liberty to take such an independent course, and the question had to be deferred. At a subse- quent meeting held this week, it is gratifying to record that an amicable settlement was arrived at. It was unani- mously decided on the proposition of a Nonconformist, the motion also being seconded by a member of the same exten- sive body, that the children of the Parish Church Schools should head 'the procession of the schools," and this com- promise was received with much satisfaction. With reference to the details of the celebration, it may be interesting to know that the members of the friendly societies will meet at the Market Hall at 10 o'clock on the morning of the 21st June (Tuesday), and to the music of several brass bands will parade the principal thoroughfares of the town, and will walk towards Halton as far as the "Crane." Be- fore dispersing at the Market Hall, selections of music are to be played by the bands. The demonstration of the schools is to take place in the afternoon, the time of aesem- bling being fixed at half-past one at the market square. After that good old tune "The old hundred" and the "National Anthem" have been sung the children will take the same route as the members of the friendly societies. Ne- gotiations are taking place for the hire of a 'field where the youngsters can disport themselves, before they proceed to their respective schools for the treat that is to be provided In the way of a substantial tea. The aged poor are aleo to have a repast toothsome and satisfying in celebration of the unique event, and the arrangements which are far from complete, are in the hands of Messrs. F. J. Norman, J. Whinyates, J. A. Smith, W. Pownall, and H. Hughes. The children's treat is under the control of the superintendents of the various Sunday schools, while the general control is vested in a committee, denominated the " Superintendence Committee," of which Messrs. T. Simister, A. Jordan, G. Kirkham, and the three secretaries, the Rev. W. Bryant, Mr. E. Marshall, and J. Whinyates, are the members. The resuecitation of the lighting of the beacon fires, which hat' been suggested in mo e than one quarter of the country, has been under consideration. The danger which now sur- I sounds the beacon rock on Runcorn Hill in the shape of a
very ugly and dangerous precipice, caused by quarrying operations, and the fact that a powder magazine is situated in the vicinity, have, so far as Runcorn is concerned, put _ .

„ the project "out et court,” and a pretty sight is thus lost to the townspeople. To make some amends for this disap- pointment, we would suggest that a display of fireworks should be given at some convenient spot. This could be done at a comparatively small cost, and nothing would give greater satisfaction. lip to the present ,£7O had beeh pro- mised towards the Cottage Hospital scheme, and about £l4O has been contributed for the" treat."

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the members of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday fore- noon. There were present Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), the Revs. T. Chambers, C. W. Wool), and Dean Finegan; Messrs. W. Middlehurst, J. Burchall, J. Jackson, J. Buckley, J. Fisher, C. B. Johnson, E. Syder, J. Kenwright, W. Tyrer, J. Matthews, J. Lowe, J. Ranson, W Swift, J Leather. barrow, J. W, Wareing, W. Gerrard, T. F. Hill, W. Daine, T. Betook, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk.) RELIEF Itirrinuis.—Mr. Hale, Workhouse master, re- ported there were 472 inmates in the Workhouse this week 474 in the preceding week, and 458 in the corresponding, week last year. A GIFT.—At a meeting of the Visiting Committee the gift of a number of books was reported from Mrs. William Tyrer, of Prescot, and the committee passed to her a hearty vote of thanks. _ _

A NHW tiORSH.—The Visiting Committee recernmended the purchase of another horse for the use of the house. In reply to a question the clerk stated t:at if the horse was purchased, it would make three which the Guardians owned. Several members objected to the proposal, and the minute was referred back. _ _

PROPOSED IMPROVElfswrs.-rat a meeting of the Build- ing Committee on the 23rd net, the committee proceeded to coneider representations Made by Mr. Henley, Local Government Boarti Inspector, at the meeting of the Guar- dians on the 28th April last, and on a former visit. Upon the motion of Mr. Fisher, seconded by Mr. Buckley, it was resolved that provision be made for not less than 80 addi- tional beds at the workhouse; and it was decided, upon the motion of Mr Lowe, seconded by Mr Buckley, that the front of the present workhouse building be altered for the above purpose,and theta boardroom and offices be erected elsewhere Mr. Hill, 'nowt' the confirmation of the minutes, and stated that the committee gave groat consideration as to the best means to carry out the alterations suggested. He observed that the recommendations were not adopted unanimously.— Mr. Johnson seconded the motion.—Mr. 141 iddlehurst said the proposed alterations to the front of the workhouse were only carried by a majority of one. He thought they might save those offices if they could build in another place where they had no building at present: and be considered those buildings were too good to be pulled down. It had been said that the cost would be about £5,000, and that went very • badly with him.. He was sure the Guardians were satisfied with the boardroom and were willing to wait to see what the Government were going to do with reference to the proposed county boards. He should never be in favour of spending £5OOO on the eve of a great alteration.—Mr. Ware- ing protested very emphatically against the unnecessary ex- penditure proposed by the Building Committee in the pur- chase of new land and the erection of new offices, dro. lie hoped they would long hesitate before committing them- selves to the scheme—Mr. Burchall suggested that the west wing should be raised so as to provide accom- modation for about 60 beds. In regard to the new offices, be asked the 71 to carefully consider before spending any money lavishly.—The Rev T. Finegan moved that the minutes be referred back, and Mr. Daine seconded the moticn —The Clerk remarked that if the Guardians pro- crastinated the Local Government Board would build the premises themselves.—After some further discussion it was decided to refer the minute back to the committee for recon- sideration.

Mars Ilona OF MEETING.—In accordance with notice given at the last meeting, the Rev T. Chambers moved that during the period from April to September, the Board should meet at 2-30 in the afternoon instead of assat present; and during the period from September to April at 10 30 in the forenoon, as at presenr.—Mr Johnson seconded the motion, which was carried after some discussion.—lt was stated that the consent of the Local Government Board would have to be obtained before the alteration could take place. TER JUBILEE TREATS.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board sanctioning the extra dietary table for the inmates of the Workhouse on the occasion of the celebration of the Queen's Jubilee on the 21st of June. In reply to a letter from the Clerk to the Guardians. the Local, Government Board wrote that they could not see their way to issue an order granting extra relief to the out- side paupers on the occasion in question_ THE TASK MISTRESS.—Miss Neannan of Mahret Bos- well, was appointed task mistress at the ;Perktionse. This was the principal business.

017TRA013 NHAR NEwcasyr.a.—About one a.m. on Tues- day, another outrage—the third of the kind within three weeks—was perpetrated at Hebburn, near Newcastle.' This time it was the police station which was the object of at- tack, and the explosive used is believed to have beta of a adore powerful type than gunpowder. The panels ef the house door of Inspector Harrison were blown out, the win- dows of the magistrates' room and the police court shat- tered, and other damage done. TIIH CANADIAN TARIFF.—TtIeSdAY'S "Liverpool Journal of Commerce " publishes in full the new Canadian tariff, in introducing which Sir Charles Tupper said there was an unworked field presenting great opportunities for its advan- tages, namely, the iron industry, the greatest industry of all countries w};ere iron and coal abound. He explained the ways in which this industry would develop and facilitate new manuf,km wee. He then showed by figures how the iron hag:luau.), of the United States exceeded the other manufactures of that country, all of which he said were far outstripped by it. Canada had imported 253,210,512 dole. worth of iron in 19 years, while she had tbe material for this under her own band. The consumption of iron through- out the world is 33ilb. per head, in Canada it is 26011„ per head,

EDWARD FAIROLOUGH, Secretary. B- OFOUGH OF EITII . ELENS.—HER —MAJESTY'S JUBILEE. At a meeting of the Town Council of this Borough, held on the 6th day of April, 1887, the following recommendations of the Special Committee appointed to repott to the Council on this subject, were adopted, viz : That Her Majesty's Jubilee be celebrated in this Borough in the following manner:- 1. That a procession through the town to the Park be or- ganised, in which the local Volunteers, the Fire Brigade, and the School Ohild^en be invited to join. 2. That on the arrival of the procession at the Park the Mayor be asked to publicly name it "The Victoria Park." 3. That a grant be made to each Elem-ntary Day School represented after the rate of Gd. for each scholar in the pro- cession who is on the school register, for the purpose of providing refreshments for the children. 4. That a medal be presented to each scholar in the pro- cession. 5. That a dinner to 500 aged poor be given. 6. That there be a display of fireworks. 7. That refreshments be provided for the Volunteers, Police, and Fire Brigade in the process on. The Aldermen and Councillors for each Ward will Act as a Local Committee for the collection of subscriptions to cover the expenditure, and donations may be paid either to them or to either of the local banks.
